#224407. BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1096 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender.
  • It has been revealed that it’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight.
  • The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It has been revealed that it’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.

The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.

Industry observers note that JLR put six registered EU designs in front of the court. The judge only needed one of them: design 005248580-0004, registered in April 2018 and covering the current Defender 110, known internally as the L663.

According to the ruling, the elements that dominate that design are the rounded “shoulders,” the rounded corners, the signature panel on the C-pillar, the rounded wheel-arch cutouts, the continuous window line, and the overall silhouette. The court found every one of them on the Ti7.

Here’s how the two SUVs compare from the same angles, using official press images from BYD and JLR:.

It has been revealed that BYD argued that the headlights, grille, bumpers, hood and side profile are all different. Not enough, stated the judge, who ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression. The court also found the Ti7 sits closer to the Defender than to older boxy SUVs like the Ford Flex, Jeep Wrangler and Mercedes G-Class.

BYD doesn’t sell the Ti7 in the EU. It told the court it has “no concrete aims” to launch it there and that the SUV can only be ordered in the UK.

Recent findings suggest that the judge didn’t buy that as a defense. By BYD’s own account, it developed the seven-seat layout for the UK and Europe, a promotional video called the Ti7 the first seven-seat SUV “in Europe,” and BYD wouldn’t commit to keeping it out of the EU. That was enough for the court to find a threat of infringement.

So BYD’s EU entities can no longer import, produce, offer, sell, store or supply the Ti7. The order kicks in one week after the ruling is formally served, and it even covers BYD’s Hungarian unit, since the judge considered it conceivable the Ti7 could come out of the new Szeged factory.

It has been revealed that the UK is a different story. The court said it has no jurisdiction over BYD UK and threw out JLR’s UK design claims, so British deliveries are still on for January 2027. That’s the one European market where BYD actually opened orders, pricing the Ti7 at £47,995, about £24,000 below the £71,840 plug-in Defender 110.

BYD mentioned it “strongly disagrees” with the judgment and will appeal, adding that the Ti7 “is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights.” JLR told AFP it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary.

Recent findings suggest that BYD has four weeks to appeal, but the injunction stays in force while it does. JLR, for its part, has six months to file a full case on the merits, or BYD can get the injunction lifted.

This whole thing started in August, when JLR had bailiffs raid BYD’s Dutch offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. The court later ordered JLR to destroy everything it seized, saying it didn’t need BYD’s internal files to make its design case. And it didn’t. JLR won on the design registration alone.

According to recent reports, the Ti7 looks like a Defender. We stated so when BYD first brought it to the UK, and so did pretty much everyone else. Chinese automakers have been building Defender lookalikes for years, but most of them stayed in China.

BYD brought one to the Defender’s home turf at a £24,000 discount, so a fight with JLR was always coming.

"...ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression.".

Recent findings suggest that really? I feel like anyone who pays even a little attention to car designs isn't going to mistake the two. The thing most people see as differentiating within the same category is the headlights, tail lights, grill - which are all significantly different.

The only real similarity is the proportions, there are a ton of similarly proportioned SUVs but that's a result of the form factor.

But honestly, all these boxy SUVs look the same to me.

In a recent development, nobody owns “boxy.” JLR even failed to trademark the classic Defender’s shape in the UK, a fight it lost in its legal battle with the Ineos Grenadier. But it registered the new Defender’s design in 2018, and that specific combination of shoulders, C-pillar panel and wheel arches is exactly what the court protected. That’s how design rights are supposed to work.

The actual business damage is small for now. The Ti7 sells roughly 30,000 units a month, almost all in China, and the UK launch goes ahead. The stock dip was about headlines more than lost Ti7 sales.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she says has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently announced a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”.

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”.

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber said.

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she said.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches said that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

According to recent reports, “PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also stated that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

In a recent development, to diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

The symptoms of PMDD may include:.

Treatment options for PMDD include prescription medications and over-the-counter treatments that may help relieve certain symptoms, such as:.

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also important.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she mentioned.

The free-to-play game set in the the universe of Arknights has been in various forms of closed tests for a while, but it finally has a release date.

The game is set to arrive simultaneously across PC, PS5, and mobile (iOS, Android) on January 22, and pre-registrations continue to be open.

Industry observers note that the developer-publisher also revealed that so far, Arknights: Endfield has had over 30 million pre-registrations worldwide since pre-registrations went live. Some players have been able to play early, of course, with the most recent opportunity being Beta Test 2.

If you’ve been following the game’s development, you’ll know that it was pretty clear we’re closer than ever to the official launch. The most recent beta build revealed off polished content, with latest animations and cutscenes.

We’ve been playing it ourselves, and we think you’re going to agree with our Arknights: Endfield character tier list. You can expect more coverage from us as we get closer to launch, and when the game actually arrives.

Though it might seem like it came out of nowhere, the game is based on the Arknights universe, itself a massive mobile game with over 100 million downloads. Endfield brings a different flavour to that world, with a mix of strategy, exploration and real-time combat, not unlike the many games created by HoYoverse.

You can pre-register yourself on the official website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the United States Forest Service has quietly published a handful of documents related to multiple, decades’ old Bigfoot sightings. While the files uploaded to the agency’s Freedom of Information Act online reading room may not offer definitive proof of the cryptid’s existence, they may help redirect unwanted political conversations at the Thanksgiving table this year.

“I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there,” an 87-year-old resident of Sanders County, Montana, told his local newspaper in 2003 after discovering some suspicious footprints. “What else could it be?”.

Another file also focuses on purported cryptid tracks in the summer of 1982. In that case, park rangers were actually dispatched to obtain plaster molds of footprints reported in Oregon’s Umatilla National Forest.Unfortunately, resource staffer Roger Baker didn’t sound impressed by what he found on June 17, 1982.

“It is my opinion that the tracks…were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus, two footed being,” Baker explained, although he did concede that the prints appeared “very natural.”.

It has been revealed that the final archival document is a local resident’s somewhat rambling personal account of the history of Petty Creek, a forested area located about 30 miles west of Missoula, Montana. Among stories of ill-fated gold prospectors, camel importation, and buried treasure, Leo Kinney tells of his own near-brush with Bigfoot. According to Kinney, he and some fellow hunters didn’t actually see the hairy biped walking around, but they saw evidence of its recent presence.

“Tracks, a strong odor, and grunting were observed,” he wrote in 1980.

The U.S. Forestry Service’s archival uploads are fun reads, but many Sasquatch believers are still reeling from the recent release of Capturing Bigfoot. Released in October, the critically acclaimed documentary delves into the story behind the Patterson–Gimlin tape. The controversial home video recording is widely considered the most famous Bigfoot sighting of all time, although the film essentially confirms once-and-for-all that the grainy footage was a carefully constructed hoax.

The Emotion Nobody Mentions When We Talk About Money

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • When Anna felt low, she went shopping.
  • According to recent reports, the calm never lasted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

When Anna felt low, she went shopping. Anna is a social worker I interviewed while researching financial well-being, and she told me about a particular kind of shop she was drawn to: soft fabrics, quiet music, a faint scent of something expensive. Her home and her workplace were busy and chaotic. In the shop, nothing bad could happen. Her biggest decision was which color coat to choose for spring.

According to recent reports, the calm never lasted. It faded almost as soon as she left, and by the time the credit card bill arrived, shame and regret had taken its place.

According to recent reports, today is Black Friday, a day built on the promise that the right purchase will make us feel better. For many of us, as for Anna, the feeling we are trying to shop away is shame.

In a recent development, it is also a feeling we rarely admit to. In a 2025 Bankrate survey, 61% of U.S. adults said they were uncomfortable discussing their bank balance. Fewer felt that way about their love life (51%), their political views (24%), or their religion (18%).

Psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett (2017) argues that emotions are constructed by the brain rather than simply triggered. I find it helpful to think of the brain as a weather forecaster. Drawing on past experience, it constantly predicts what our bodily sensations mean, and it revises the forecast as upcoming information comes in.

A knot in your stomach before a job interview could be hunger, dread, or excitement. Which one you feel depends partly on how your brain has learned to read situations like this one.

Many of us have years of money forecasts shaped by tension and secrecy at home. Opening a bill or splitting a restaurant check can call up an old forecast before we have even looked at the numbers. Often, that forecast is for shame.

Internal shame is the voice that claims, “I’m bad with money.” It treats missing financial skills as a personal flaw, and a rare one. Everyone else seems to manage. If I struggle, it must say something about who I am.

Sources indicate that this belief often starts early. Many of the middle-aged adults I meet, particularly women, tell me nobody talked openly about money with them when they were growing up. They learned through costly mistakes, and each mistake seemed to confirm that something was wrong with them.

Recent findings suggest that external shame is about how others see us. In 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that the ancient Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen, yet in his own day, a respectable laborer would be ashamed to appear in public without a linen shirt. What counts as a necessity depends partly on what we need to avoid being looked down on.

Industry observers note that swedish researcher Bengt Starrin and colleagues (2009) tested this idea in a survey of more than 5,600 adults. Both financial stress and experiences of being shamed predicted psychosocial ill-health, and people who reported both were the most affected. Having too little money is hard, and feeling diminished because of it adds to the harm.

Sources indicate that money shame is not limited to poverty. It can be strongest when, by all appearances, there should be enough.

Sources indicate that ann-Marie is a journalist with three books to her name and steady work for well-known magazines. She is a single mother of two, widowed when her daughters were small. She still pays a large mortgage on a country house she has been unable to sell, while renting in the city near her daughters’ music schools. Her income is reasonable, but she has no buffer. One unexpected bill sets her back, and she knows what it means to stretch her last ten euros across a week of groceries.

Recent findings suggest that she skips most social events because they cost money. She never mentions her worries to her daughters, which makes it hard to explain why they rarely travel or why her laptop comes along on weekends. To others, her life looks successful. She keeps the rest to herself.

Ann-Marie is far from alone. In the American Psychological Association’s Stress in America 2023 survey, 82% of adults aged 18 to 34 named money as a significant source of stress.

Industry observers note that shame is a social emotion. It probably evolved to keep us in good standing with our group, but when it takes hold, it does undeniable damage. A meta-analysis of 108 studies found that shame is more strongly linked to depressive symptoms than guilt is (Kim et al., 2011).

With money, shame can also make the original problem worse. Joe Gladstone and colleagues (2021) studied this using bank records, longitudinal surveys, and comparisons of identical twins. Across six studies, people who felt financial shame were more likely to disengage from their finances. That disengagement led to poorer financial decisions, which deepened their hardship. The researchers call this a financial shame spiral, something many of us are familiar with in our daily lives.

Fear of judgment adds to the feeling of shame. In a study of middle-class consumers in debt, those who expected to be stigmatized hid their debt from friends and family, put off seeking help, and even spent more in social situations to keep up appearances (Moorhouse et al., 2023).

Industry observers note that it’s a bit like a leak you are too embarrassed to report. The longer you hide it, the more damage it does to the house.

In a recent development, the shame researcher Brené Brown (2007) describes empathy as the antidote to shame. Here are some ways to put that into practice with money.

Start with understanding rather than resolutions. Vowing to take control and cut out every bad habit rarely lasts. It helps more to ask how you got here. What did you learn about money as a child? What might your spending or avoidance have been protecting you from?

Industry observers note that name the feeling. When a money task makes you tense, try saying to yourself, “This is shame.” Brain-imaging research reveals that putting feelings into words reduces activity in the amygdala, a region involved in emotional alarm (Lieberman et al., 2007). Naming the feeling may give your forecast a chance to update.

In a recent development, remember that financial skills are learned. If you never learned them, that reflects what you were taught, and claims nothing about your character. In Gladstone’s research, an intervention built around affirming acts of kindness weakened the link between shame and disengagement.

It has been revealed that talk to someone. In a field experiment, people who took a financial course alongside others in the same situation paid off more debt than people in the control group. Among those most afraid of judgment, learning in a group also improved well-being more than learning privately did (Moorhouse et al., 2023). A friend, a partner, or a financial counselor can all be a starting point.

It has been revealed that for Anna, the work was learning to find calm without a fresh purchase. Part of that was looking a little further ahead and asking what feeling each shopping trip would leave behind. That question is worth asking today, before checkout.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that an international team of scientists conducting a deep-sea survey of the Great Australian Bight discovered the clam.
  • In a recent development, they found V.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the fact that a new clam species (Vaticinaria gulicola) was discovered where the sun does not shine may be the least interesting thing about this bivalve. V. gulicola lives inside of a deep-sea urchin. The clam appears to have made a little home for itself inside the urchin’s oesophagus, the tube that runs through the center of the urchin’s body and into the intestine. A study recently published in the journal ZooKeys details this highly unusual partnership.

Industry observers note that an international team of scientists conducting a deep-sea survey of the Great Australian Bight discovered the clam. The survey studied the seafloor at depths of 656 to 16,404 feet deep and uncovered 66,721 invertebrates representing 1,267 species. About a third of these species are believed to be newly introduced to science—including this quirky clam.

In a recent development, they found V. gulicola along the abyssal seafloor at depths of about 13,000 to 16,400 feet. At this depth, sunlight cannot penetrate the water column. During these deep trawls, the team found clams equipped with threads for attaching to a host, but did not see any hosts. Additional searching revealed more clams lodged inside thin, slippery tubes. They analyzed the DNA of these tubes and discovered that they were the oesophagus of the urchin Carnarechinus clypeatus.

Recent findings suggest that “We were absolutely stunned to find this bivalve living inside the throat of a deepwater sea urchin,” Paul Valentich-Scott, a study co-author and marine malacologist at the Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History, said in a statement. “A Russian scientist [Alexander Mironov] originally thought these clams were being eaten by the sea urchin, but we later determined that it was actually living inside the oesophagus.”.

It has been revealed that mironov had noticed clams inside the urchin’s gut as far back as the 1970s and 1990s. The team also found related clams living inside of a specimen of the same urchin that was collected during the Challenger Expedition (1872 to 1876), where they had gone unnoticed for over a century.

Most clam species that live with other animals cling to the outside of their host. Endocommensalism, or living inside of the host, is more rare. The latest clam’s genus Vaticinaria is only the second clam genus of its superfamily known to live this way.

“Endocommensalism is extremely rare in galeommatids and all bivalves,” Valentich-Scott added. “Most commensal bivalves attach to the outside of their host. This upcoming species lives inside its throat.”.

Sources indicate that this latest clam indicates no obvious adaptations to life inside a host. It is about 0.74 inches long, which is large for its group, and has a shell that closes fully. The species name gulicola comes from the Latin word for “throat” and “inhabitant.” Much about the clam remains unknown and will require further study.

Sources indicate that “We know very little about this newly introduced species or its sea urchin host,” said Valentich-Scott. “The host sea urchin has never been collected intact, so we really don’t even know what it looks like. We have no idea how this bivalve can live inside the throat of the urchin, or what it eats.”.

The team suspects that the clams can feed off the nutrient-rich sediment that the urchin eats, but this hasn’t been studied. Further deep-sea sampling should reveal more about this clam and other unusual creatures of the deep-sea.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Subaru vehicles are known for their dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) capabilities, but to cut costs, the company is now offering front-wheel-drive (FWD) versions on select electric models.

The Uncharted EV went on sale earlier this year as a smaller, sportier entry-level electric crossover positioned below the Solterra.

It was also the first Subaru model in about 30 years not to come with standard all-wheel drive. After unveiling the Uncharted EV last summer, Subaru said, “For buyers focused on affordability and range, the entry-level Uncharted Premium FWD model will be offered in limited numbers.”.

Apparently, it wasn’t too limited. The 2027 Uncharted EV is now on sale, still with the base Premium FWD model equipped with a single 221-horsepower front-mounted electric motor.

Higher-priced Uncharted trims, including the Sport and GT, are upgraded with Subaru’s Symmetrical All-Wheel Drive system with X-Mode, delivering a combined 338 horsepower.

The 2027 Subaru Uncharted EV Premium FWD starts at $34,995, while the Sport and GT are priced from $39,795 and $43,795, respectively.

In the US, the 2027 Solterra and larger Trailseeker are still equipped with standard AWD, but Subaru is introducing fresh FWD (4×2) variants in some markets at a lower price point.

In comparison, the 2027 Subaru Solterra and Trailseeker EV start at $38,495 and $39,995, respectively.

Subaru opened preorders for its new 2027 electric range in Spain, including the Unchartered, Solterra, and E-Outback, which is sold as the Trailseeker in the US.

All of which will be available with a lower-priced FWD variant. Like the Uncharted, Subaru will still offer AWD on higher-priced Solterra and E-Outback trims.

The new Subaru Uncharted (4×2) starts at €26,525 ($28,900), the Solterra (4×2) starts at €35,025 ($38,200), and the E-Outback (4×2) starts at €36,525 ($39,800) in Spain, including subsidies, discounts, and other incentives.

Preorders are open for the Uncharted, while the Solterra and E-Outback are expected to launch in mid-2027.

Will Subaru expand FWD (4×2) to other vehicles and markets, like the US? The Uncharted is still Subaru’s only EV sold with standard FWD. The 2027 Solterra and Trailseeker are equipped with AWD and X-Mode.

According to recent reports, for a small electric car driven on pavement I prefer RWD, which offers less complexity, better uphill traction, and a tighter turning circle. I love the handling of my last two cars, a RWD Miata and a RWD BMW i3 (old style).

Subaru is already selling considerably more EVs in the US, with three affordable, practical electric SUVs: the Uncharted, Solterra, and Trailseeker.

Lord of Hatred delivers a fresh campaign that continues the mainline story, picking up from where Vessel of Hatred left off. Mephisto, the eponymous Lord of Hatred, has seemingly finally escaped imprisonment to rule over Sanctuary.

Lord of Hatred is the second Diablo 4 expansion, and it will be available on PC, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S on April 28.

It’s always a major deal when we get a upcoming Diablo expansion, especially for a game as starved of fresh (major) content as Diablo 4 has been. But perhaps the biggest piece of news out of the Lord of Hatred reveal is that the expansion is bringing not one, but two new classes to the game.

The first of which is The Paladin, whereas the second is being kept under wraps. Even more surprising is that The Paladin is playable right now for anyone who pre-purchases the expansion. This is a well-timed shadow drop, especially given that Diablo 4’s latest season has just kicked off.

It has been revealed that the expansion adds a latest region to the world: Skovos, which is where the events of the new campaign will be taking place. This is the first time Skovos has been in a Diablo game. The region is of major significance to the world and lore of the series, as it is the birthplace of the firstborn, home of Lilith and Inaruis.

Lord of Hatred brings a decent number of major systems to Diablo 4. The endgame is getting a big overhaul, headlined by the upcoming War Plans feature. Through this, you can effectively design your own endgame grind, creating challenges based on the activities you like and earning rewards along the way.

Endgame activities now also feature their own skill trees, which can be progressed through by creating War Prepares for your character featuring each activity. The latest endgame activity, Echoing Hatred, is something of horde mode where you must defend against unrelenting waves of enemies.

It has been revealed that none of that matters without loot, of course, and the upcoming expansion is bringing back the Horadric Cube, and adding set bonuses using the Talisman system. The long-awaited and highly-requested Loot Filter is also coming to the game with the release of the expansion.

Recent findings suggest that beyond itemisation, each class’ skill tree will grow with new bonus skill variants. In fact, the entire skill system is being reworked for all classes - though details are a little sparse at the moment.

In a recent development, you can also expect the level cap to go up, which is very likely necessary to fit all the latest skills and various systems. Blizzard offered a deep dive into the new Paladin class, which you see on the official blog.

Turkeys may be getting all of the bird hype this week, but plenty is still going on in the reality show that is the bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) world.

Industry observers note that just before the sun rose over Big Bear Valley in southern California on Monday morning, Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) cameras picked up the sounds of eagle chortles throughout the area. The sounds continued as the sun came up over the nest that typically belongs to an internet-famous bald eagle dad named Shadow and his late partner, Jackie.

In a recent development, “Eagles vocalize for many different reasons. It could be to communicate territory, a danger warning, mating, food necessity or merely social contact. Their tone is that of a whistling chatter-like chirp, making it easy to differentiate them with their distinctive, high pitched sounds,” FOBBV writes.

Industry observers note that the cameras also picked up two unknown soaring eagles, and some ravens scrounging around in the nest. By Monday afternoon, two bald eagles followed each other onto the Lookout Snag, a tree near the nest. While it is not clear which eagles were there, a familiar face was spotted just before sunset. Kaydee, the four-year-old banded female eagle who has been seen near Shadow since August, swooped onto the nest for the first time in several days.

“Kaydee made a welcome visit to the nest. She poked around a bit, before showing us some beautiful closeups, then exiting through the back porch,” FOBBV claims. “We can all agree what a welcome sight it was to see Kaydee. It’s a gentle reminder that if we just wait, there are newly introduced surprises each and every day.”.

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Shadow has recently been spotted with another female eagle nicknamed Big Beautiful Visitor (BBV) by some fans. Any eggs are generally laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow, Kaydee, or any other eagle couple that takes over the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Significant Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

In a recent development, kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee right now has a black spot on her head, but that may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers, who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center noted that she was in unstable condition on August 9.

Recent findings suggest that jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

Sources indicate that A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Substantial Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

Earlier this month, the Ojai Raptor Center announced a “room filled with kindness,” that is covered with thousands of letters, drawings, cards, and well-wishes they have received in honor of Jackie.

#224395. Tech Report: What Elizabeth Holmes's Stare Doesn’t Say

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (827 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What Elizabeth Holmes's Stare Doesn’t Say

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything, the camera cuts to a tight close-up of the upper half of Elizabeth Holmes’s face.
  • It has been revealed that holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, has the same wide blue eyes and unblinking gaze.
  • Blinking is a coordinated sensorimotor action that protects the eyes while reflecting shifts in attention and cognitive load.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything, the camera cuts to a tight close-up of the upper half of Elizabeth Holmes’s face. Her large blue eyes hold Fielder’s gaze for an extraordinarily long time without blinking. It was quite distracting. I found myself counting the seconds between blinks and trying to match them. I couldn’t keep up.

It has been revealed that holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, has the same wide blue eyes and unblinking gaze. It was unnerving to watch them even in the safety of my own living room.

Blinking is a coordinated sensorimotor action that protects the eyes while reflecting shifts in attention and cognitive load. Adults typically blink about 14 to 17 times per minute, with each blink lasting roughly 100 to 300 milliseconds.

People naturally blink less when they’re working hard to focus. Studies in cognitive and auditory neuroscience show that people systematically blink less during moments of high cognitive demand. For example, people blink less in noisy environments so they don’t miss visual cues like lip movement.

In a recent development, holmes and Evans don’t just blink less; their wide-eyed look shows white around the iris. This effect comes from how far the eyelids open, not how often they close. Put the two together—wide-open lids and a low blink rate—and you get a jarring laser-focused stare. The iris, an orb floating in a white sea of sclera.

Research by Tamami Nakano found that people watching someone speak tend to sync their blinks with the speaker's. When I tried to match Holmes's blinks and failed, I was consciously doing what viewers do without noticing.

Psychologists Sharon Leal and Aldert Vrij found that people blinked less when they lied and blinked more than usual right afterward. Their 2008 research concluded that lying is cognitively demanding. Blinking slows while the lie is being told, then rebounds once it's over.

I’m not suggesting Holmes is a liar. Someone who blinks less might be lying, but they may also be concentrating, self-conscious in front of a camera, on medication, or simply a person who blinks less than average. A low blink rate, in and of itself, suggests someone may be working hard. It doesn’t tell us at what.

Recent findings suggest that holmes’s stare also reminded me of Anthony Hopkins’s Oscar-winning performance as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs. Hopkins said in an interview that he deliberately minimized blinking while playing the cannibalistic serial killer. The result was an unflinching performance that made Lecter feel oddly calm, predatory, and menacing.

While popular culture associates unblinking stares with sociopathy, the research doesn’t support it. In fact, some studies suggest that people high in psychopathic traits pay less attention to other people’s eyes, not more. An unblinking stare is not a reliable indicator of a personality disorder. It can be an effective tool for an actor or for a young founder delivering a TEDMED talk, as Holmes did in 2014. But it’s not diagnostic.

In the 2005 bestseller Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking, author Malcolm Gladwell argued that snap judgments and first impressions formed within the first two seconds can be just as accurate as slow, deliberate analysis. “There can be as much value in the blink of an eye as in months of rational analysis,” he wrote.

Gladwell wasn’t writing about literal blinking, but he attached a condition that matters here: fast judgments are trustworthy only when they’re grounded in real experience.

According to recent reports, my first reaction to Holmes and Evans was a snap judgment. I don’t have any real expertise in reading blink rates. What I have is a cultural script (Hannibal Lecter, the wide-eyed villain) and an expectation about conversational rhythm, which includes blinking and looking away occasionally.

That doesn’t make my unease any less valid. It was real information about me. It told me that Holmes’s stare had broken a social rhythm, and that I was primed to read that break as menace.

In a recent development, the documentary title promises we can see everything. The close-up on Holmes’s eyes reminds us we can’t. All we can see is that she isn’t blinking. We can’t see why.

Gillespie, S. M., Rotshtein, P., Wells, L. J., Beech, A. R., & Mitchell, I. J. (2015). Psychopathic traits are associated with reduced attention to the eyes of emotional faces among adult male non-offenders. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 9, 552.

According to recent reports, gladwell, M. (2005). Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking. Little, Brown.

Leal, S., & Vrij, A. (2008). Blinking during and after lying. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 32(4), 187–194.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, somehow, after all these years, there are still a considerable number of vehicles equipped with Takata airbags, though their number should be considerably lower in the near future. Honda just issued a recall for 810,592 cars equipped with Takata airbags that could rupture due to propellant degradation caused by high humidity.

In a recent development, according to documents filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the recall covers some 2013 Acura RDX, ILX, Honda CR-V, Civic, and Accord models. The affected Accords and Acuras are all from the 2013 model year, while the CR-V and Civic populations include both 2012 and 2013 vehicles.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

The NHTSA documents show that the affected vehicles are equipped with airbag inflators that use a phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate propellant, which is intended to control moisture within the inflator. Over time, exposure to high humidity and repeated temperature changes can cause the inflator to become brittle. When the brittle inflators are deployed, they could turn into projectiles that shoot metal fragments through the cabin, potentially injuring or killing occupants.

The recall comes after years of investigation and analysis by Honda, which was routinely shared with NHTSA. The recall documents show that on November 19, 2026, Honda determined that the inflators posed enough of a risk to warrant the latest recall.

In a recent development, owners of affected models will be contacted by mail and urged to bring their vehicle to a Honda or Acura dealership. Dealer technicians will replace the driver and passenger airbag inflators with a different model for free. Dealers have already been notified of the recall, with owner notification letters scheduled to be sent on December 18. Owners concerned that their car might be included in the recall can check on the NHTSA recalls site as well as NHTSA’s dedicated Takata airbag recall page.

Does Menopausal Hormone Therapy Lower Dementia Risk? Timing and Genetics May Hold the Answer

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.
  • The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.
  • The findings could offer fresh insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women who have longer reproductive life spans or use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) may have better brain health as they age, according to a new study.

The research, published November 4 in Neurology, found that longer lifetime exposure to estrogen was associated with fewer signs of damage to small blood vessels in the brain.

The findings could offer fresh insights into the relationship between estrogen and brain aging, particularly as women account for approximately two-thirds of Alzheimer’s disease cases worldwide.

Researchers also found that certain associations between hormone therapy and brain health differed depending on whether women carried a genetic variant associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

In a recent development, however, the relationship between estrogen and brain health is complex. While the findings suggest that longer estrogen exposure may be associated with healthier brain aging, they do not establish that hormone therapy can prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

The researchers drew data from the Gothenburg H70-1944 Birth Cohort, a longitudinal study of 1,203 individuals born in 1944 who resided in Gothenburg, Sweden.

The final cohort included 352 cisgender women, with an average age of 70, who had no neurological disorders and reliable self-reported data on their estrogen exposure.

Sources indicate that individual estrogen exposure was measured through structured interviews. It included:.

The researchers used this information as a proxy for lifetime estrogen exposure, though the study didn’t measure actual hormone levels.

Participants were also given a brain MRI at baseline and then again at a 5-year follow-up.

The researchers found that those with a longer reproductive span had a lower risk of small vessel disease (SVD). Participants with a longer reproductive life span had an 8% lower risk of having two or more signs of SVD. However, later menopause, rather than earlier menstruation, appeared to be the main driver of this association.

Those who used MHT also tended to have fewer signs of SVD and better microstructural integrity in the white matter.

In a recent development, in individuals who carried the APOE-ε4 variant, which increases a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease, MHT was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease. However, there was no association for those without this variant.

The researchers noted that longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that estrogen has several important effects on the brain that may help support cognitive health.

It influences communication between brain cells, supports the brain’s ability to use glucose for energy, helps regulate neurotransmitters, and plays a role in maintaining healthy blood vessels and reducing inflammation and oxidative stress.

Industry observers note that “As estrogen levels decline during menopause, some of these protective effects may diminish. Replacing estrogen closer to the menopause transition could potentially help preserve some of these functions during a vulnerable period for brain health,” he said. “While these findings are encouraging, MHT has not been proven to prevent Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.”.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed and noted, “Starting menopausal hormone therapy earlier in the menopause transition may help minimize some changes by supporting the brain during this period of hormonal fluctuation.”.

“There is growing interest in whether early estrogen therapy may also help reduce the long-term risk of Alzheimer’s disease, although more research is needed before we can establish that benefit,” she added.

Ross told Healthline that this research reinforces the importance of recognizing menopause as more than a reproductive or hormonal transition.

“We know that women are disproportionately affected by dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and some women experience noticeable cognitive changes beginning in perimenopause,” she mentioned. “If future research confirms that starting hormone therapy earlier can help protect long-term cognitive health, it could influence how we approach menopause treatment and encourage more proactive conversations between women and their healthcare providers.”.

“The goal should be to individualize treatment based on a woman’s symptoms, medical history, and overall health rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach,” Ross added.

Trinh agreed that an individualized approach to menopause management is important.

In a recent development, “This does not mean that every woman should start hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Instead, it highlights the importance of understanding which women might benefit, when treatment should begin, and which formulations are most appropriate,” he said. “Factors such as age, time since menopause, cardiovascular risk, metabolic health, family history, and potentially genetic factors may all help guide future recommendations.”.

“We still need stronger clinical evidence before changing current prescribing guidelines specifically for dementia prevention,” Trinh added.

Industry observers note that the Belgian developer is returning to the series it created with Divinity, a non-numbered sequel that’s designed for new and veteran players alike. The announcement was entirely cinematic, setting the tone for what looks to be the next massive thing in the space.

Larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before. This is the next project from the Baldur’s Gate 3 team, after all, so there’s understandably immense anticipation for it.

According to recent reports, “This marks the beginning of something with more breadth, depth, and intimacy than anything we’ve created before. Beyond that, there’s precious little that’s been revealed for Divinity so far. We don’t know what platforms it’s going to be coming to, nor do we even have a release target. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Red Dog Mine in Alaska burns about 40,000 gallons of diesel a day to keep one of the world’s largest zinc mines running, and now, an 8.8-megawatt (MW) solar farm and battery storage will help cut that fuel use.

Industry observers note that the Alaska Energy Authority’s board unanimously approved a nearly $5 million loan for the project through its Power Project Fund. Tugliq Red Dog1 will build, own, and operate the roughly $35 million solar project and sell the electricity to mine operator Teck Alaska. The state’s loan review claims site work began in June and expects the solar and storage to come online in October 2028.

In a recent development, red Dog sits about 105 miles north of the Arctic Circle, on land owned by NANA, an Iñupiat-owned Alaska Native corporation. The array would be larger than any solar farm operating in Alaska today, as KOTZ’s Desiree Hagen reported for Alaska Public Media. Hagen reported that the aims call for more than 15,000 panels across around 30 acres.

According to recent reports, the mine gets all its power from on-site diesel generators. In summer, it can draw so much electricity that Teck has to cut power elsewhere at the site. The solar array and the 8.8 MW, 15 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery will give the operator another source of power during those crunches.

In a recent development, the state of Alaska expects the solar and storage project to cover about 5% of the zinc mine’s electricity needs under its current operating proposal. The project could do even more after mining ends, covering about 90% of the site’s annual electricity needs.

Cost to import sun to a remote Alaskan village 0, cost to import diesel quite high.

A 500W panel weighs 60 lbs about the same as 9 gallons of diesel. 500W panel generates 750kwh of electricity a year each and every year for 20 years. 9 gallons of diesel gives you 350kwh of thermal energy which yields varying amounts of desired output.

Teck expects the mine’s existing deposits to support operations through 2031, and it’s studying whether to develop two nearby deposits. If that expansion goes ahead, the state projects the solar and battery project would cover about 3% of the larger operation’s electricity needs. If mining ends, demand will drop sharply, but the site will still need electricity for cleanup and long-term water treatment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species.
  • “This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species. For its tenacity in finding food, a small mink (Neogale vison)  walking around Anan Creek wins the On a Mission Award.

“This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write. “It seemed unconcerned by nearby humans, completely focused on the small crabs and other nibbles it could get ahold of. It was on a mission to eat!”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

In addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home. Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), the Alexander Archipelago wolf (Canis lupus ligoni), and the Sitka black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), coho (Oncorhynchus kisutch), pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), sockeye  (Oncorhynchus nerka), and chum (Oncorhynchus keta). These five fish species help feed the bears and other mammals and birds who gather here.

Industry observers note that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#224386. Tech Report: What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future

Tech Report: What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • We look back at the year, count our achievements, contemplate our disappointments, and begin constructing a better version of ourselves for January.
  • This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 27, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

December invites a peculiar ritual. We look back at the year, count our achievements, contemplate our disappointments, and begin constructing a better version of ourselves for January. In 2026, artificial intelligence became an increasingly available accomplice in this exercise. It can summarize our accomplishments, identify inefficiencies, suggest resolutions, and construct an impressively optimized roadmap for 2027. Yet imagine reviewing your year differently. Instead of asking what went according to plan, consider what happened because it didn't. The conversation you never intended to have. The problem that refused to disappear. The project that demanded more than you thought you could give. Perhaps the moments that changed you most were precisely those that resisted optimization.

This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance. We have become extraordinarily good at eliminating inconvenience, yet psychological flourishing may depend partly on experiences that cannot be anticipated, accelerated, or outsourced. The interplay between friction and flow offers a way to understand why.

We generally prefer ease, but our relationship with effort is more complicated than this preference suggests. A 2024 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin confirmed that mental effort is commonly experienced as unpleasant. Yet research published in Cognition in 2025, drawing on six studies involving 2,883 participants, found that exerting effort can increase an activity's perceived meaningfulness. One experiment compared writing with and without ChatGPT assistance. Greater effort contributed to meaning only up to a point. Still, the findings illuminate something that efficiency calculations routinely overlook. We may dislike the difficulty of an experience while valuing what that difficulty allows us to become. This paradox helps explain why flow, the state of intense absorption described by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, cannot simply be manufactured by making everything easier.

In a recent development, A meta-analysis examining the relationship between challenge and skill found that their balance contributes significantly to flow, alongside clear goals and a sense of control. More recent research in Communications Psychology emphasizes autonomy and the personal significance of an activity. Flow emerges through engagement with something sufficiently demanding to absorb us, yet manageable enough to sustain participation. The pianist needs a piece that stretches her abilities; the writer needs an idea that refuses to settle into easy sentences. Friction provides the resistance through which skill becomes experience, and experience becomes satisfaction.

Now consider an algorithmic environment increasingly designed to anticipate our desires and remove obstacles before we encounter them. Recommendations narrow our search; predictive systems streamline our choices, and generative AI can produce results without requiring us to navigate the uncertainties of creation. Such assistance can be enormously beneficial, particularly when it relieves unnecessary burdens. Yet when friction disappears indiscriminately, we risk losing opportunities for the very engagement that makes flow possible. A life engineered for effortless outcomes might become strangely impoverished in the experiences through which we develop competence, confidence, and curiosity. This remains a psychological risk rather than an established destiny, but it raises an essential question: Are we optimizing the quality of our experiences, or merely the speed with which we move through them?

Recent findings suggest that research suggests that our conventional understanding of a good life may itself be incomplete. Some consider psychological richness a dimension of well-being alongside happiness and meaning. A related 2025 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences describes psychologically rich lives as those containing diverse, interesting, and perspective-changing experiences. To be clear, such experiences are not uniformly pleasant. An unfamiliar place, a challenging encounter, or an unexpected reversal may enlarge our understanding precisely because it disrupts familiar assumptions. This opens an interesting perspective on December's customary stocktaking.

The experiences that made 2026 psychologically rich may be poorly represented by our conventional measures of success. A friendship deepened through disagreement, an unexpected professional change, or an abandoned plan that opened an unforeseen possibility might have contributed more to personal development than another efficiently completed task. Of course, hardship is not inherently beneficial. Financial insecurity, discrimination, illness, and exhausting administrative obstacles can diminish well-being and restrict agency. The distinction worth preserving is between friction that erodes our ability to flourish and friction that invites us to exercise it.

The approaching newly introduced year makes this distinction painfully relevant. Research on the fresh start effect shows that temporal landmarks, including the beginning of a new year, can motivate humans to pursue aspirations. Perhaps we could use this psychological opening differently in December 2026? Rather than designing another year around the elimination of effort, we might ask which forms of friction deserve a place in our lives. Which difficulties strengthen our abilities? Which uncertainties invite discovery? Which activities would lose their meaning if someone—or something—completed them for us?

In a recent development, the challenge is to choose meaningful friction deliberately, without turning everyday life into an obstacle course. BLISS offers five practical ways to cultivate that judgment.

B — Begin before borrowing. Give your own imagination an opportunity to work before requesting an algorithmic solution.

Industry observers note that L — Let learning take time. Preserve activities in which gradual improvement brings satisfaction, even when shortcuts are readily available.

Sources indicate that I — Invite the unfamiliar. Explore beyond personalized recommendations; seek perspectives and experiences that might challenge established preferences.

Industry observers note that S — Stay with the struggle. When a difficulty is productive, resist the urge to eliminate it immediately. Allow yourself the satisfaction of finding a way through.

S — Save space for surprise. Leave some time unplanned, some questions unanswered, and some possibilities unexplored until they present themselves.

Recent findings suggest that we can welcome intelligent technologies that reduce unnecessary suffering while protecting the experiences that develop natural intelligence. An increasingly capable algorithmic future need not become a frictionless one, provided we retain the freedom and capacity to choose where human effort matters. As 2026 ends, perhaps the most meaningful resolution for 2027 is not to become more efficient, organized, or productive. It is to become more attentive to what makes life worth living. The winding path through unfamiliar territory may take longer, demand more, and occasionally lead somewhere unexpected. Yet it may also reveal capacities and possibilities that a perfectly optimized route would never allow us to discover.

We need friction to find flow. And sometimes, the detour is the destination.

#224384. Can Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre Technology Replace Drive Modes?

Can Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre Technology Replace Drive Modes?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout.
  • That information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data.
  • "This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout. The tires use a sensor that looks a lot like a Dexcom G7 to feed temperature, air pressure, acceleration, and identification data to a vehicle's computers.

That information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data. For example, swap your summer tires for squishier winter rubber, and a compatible car could recognize the change and automatically adjust how its electronic controls intervene, leaving you free to imagine a world where maybe we all just drove better.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

"This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani. The sensor, weighing just 13 grams, is bonded to the tire's inner liner beneath the tread using a specially developed adhesive and rubber housing. The process was developed using learnings from Pirelli's Noise Cancelling System, which uses foam inside the tire to absorb sound waves and reduce cabin vibration. The sensor must survive extreme temperatures, constant flexing, and the insane lateral g-forces that tires are susceptible to at over 200 mph. Engineers explained that its battery is designed to outlast the tire and enters a low-power sleep mode during extended storage.

The more inspiring part is what the car does with the information it gathers. As we found in our recent all-weather tire comparison test, summer, winter, and all-season tires perform dramatically differently. Yet a vehicle's electronic controls are generally calibrated around its original equipment, using things like wheel speed sensors that aren’t as close to the road surface as the Cyber Tyre. Instead, it identifies the specific tire installed at each corner, allowing it to use different wheel-slip targets. And with the sensor attached to the inside of the tire, the data informing those systems is closer to the road surface than ever.

We sampled the technology at Las Vegas Motor Speedway in two Mercedes-AMG GT63 S four-doors wearing Cyber Tyre-equipped P Zero MS all-season tires.

The first exercise had us pin the throttle through a corner from 40 mph using three different traction-control calibrations, all on the same P Zero MS all-season tires. The first, intended for ultra-high-performance summer tires, was overly restrictive, cutting power before the tires could deliver much acceleration. The second, calibrated for winter tires, permitted considerably more wheelspin, making the AMG easy to slide. Despite that setting being the most fun (and our favorite), Cyber Tyre delivered a happy medium, allowing more controlled acceleration without either extreme.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

According to recent reports, this is where Cyber Tyre begins to make the case against selectable drive modes. The same car, wearing the same tires, just behaved three different ways without any mechanical changes. It's not going to replace the button that stiffens your dampers or changes your exhaust note, but it could eventually make some traction-related settings redundant.

Recent findings suggest that the second AMG demonstrated ABS braking from 65 mph. With Cyber Tyre integration active, our stopping distance improved by 0.9 meter, or about three feet, according to Pirelli's instrumentation. That's not dramatically different, but still a measurable improvement.

Of course, these demonstrations weren't proof that Cyber Tyre can outperform a conventional system already calibrated for the correct tires. And the technology isn't smart enough to know it's snowing just because the tires are cold. But the distinction is that Cyber Tyre can give the car information about its tires without the driver doing anything. That could be super useful as tires wear, temperatures change, or owners swap between summer and winter sets. Pirelli is also developing tire-wear estimates using its sensor data, which could prove useful for fleet operators managing hundreds of vehicles.

According to recent reports, pirelli and Bosch unveiled their development partnership in 2024, and the technology has already appeared in vehicles from McLaren and Pagani. Pirelli executives say a substantially higher-volume application should be announced in the first half of 2027, with production expected in 2028. So it's possible this tech could arrive in models as common as a Ford pickup.

Industry observers note that pirelli is also investing approximately $1.2 billion to expand its Rome, Georgia, manufacturing facility, where Cyber Tyre-equipped products will be produced alongside conventional tires. By 2033, the organization expects annual production capacity to reach six million tires and plans to add up to 1000 engineering jobs.

They also recently declared that China's state-owned Sinochem, formerly Pirelli's largest shareholder, reduced its ownership to 13.6 percent in November. The Italian government has restricted Sinochem's influence and specifically prohibited sharing Cyber Tyre data with entities connected to the Chinese government. Following those governance changes, Pirelli received U.S. authorization to market the technology here. Not that anyone was worried about a Pagani Utopia Roadster being a boon of classified information.

Cyber Tyre isn't about to take the Ford Bronco's G.O.A.T. modes out back to shoot them. There are plenty of reasons to let drivers decide how their cars behave. But after experiencing three dramatically different calibrations in the same AMG, it's easy to see why some of those decisions might eventually be better left to the car. Just make sure we’re able to fully disable them.

Austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

#224382. Industry News: The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The e-bike industry has a horsepower problem

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.
  • Industry observers note that spend enough time browsing new e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power.
  • If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was a time when 750 watts sounded like a lot of power for an electric bicycle.

These days, apparently those are rookie numbers.

Industry observers note that spend enough time browsing new e-bike launches and you’ll inevitably stumble across bikes advertising 1,000W, 1,500W, 2,000W, or even higher power. Dual-motor models have turned the spec sheet into an arms race, with manufacturers seemingly competing to see who can slap the biggest number onto the product page.

If you ask me, the e-bike industry is developing a horsepower problem.

To be clear, I’m not anti-power. I’ve ridden everything from dainty 250W European commuter bikes to electric motorcycles with enough power to rearrange your chest cavity. Powerful electric two-wheelers are fun, period.

But there’s a difference between building a powerful electric two-wheeler and pretending that every powerful electric two-wheeler is still an electric bicycle.

In the US, the widely adopted three-class e-bike system generally tops out at 20 mph (32 km/h) for Class 1 and Class 2 e-bikes and 28 mph (45 km/h) for Class 3, with some minor exceptions, and 750 watts has long been a common benchmark for the motor power limit.

Yet browse online e-bike retailers today and you’ll find plenty of machines advertised with motors well beyond that figure, often capable of speeds far beyond normal electric bicycle classifications.

Sometimes there’s a disclaimer explaining that the bike is intended for “off-road use.” Sometimes there’s a software setting that supposedly limits it for street riding.

And sometimes people just sort of squint at the pedals and agree to keep calling it an electric bicycle.

The problem isn’t that 2,000W electric two-wheelers exist. I love lightweight electric motorcycles and mopeds, or what some are beginning to refer to as ‘e-motos’, despite that terminology having its own concerns. So sure, those bikes are great and there is a time and place for such power. The problem is that the industry increasingly seems afraid to call them what they are.

Part of the blame belongs to consumers – to us.

Recent findings suggest that E-bike shopping has become increasingly spec-sheet driven, and wattage provides an incredibly easy number to compare. If ‘Bike A’ has a 750W motor and ‘Bike B’ costs the same but advertises 1,500W, it’s easy to assume ‘Bike B’ is twice as good. This is especially true for younger riders who lack a deeper understanding of how e-bikes work, and just want something powerful and fast to impress their friends after school. They beg their parents for the latest models with the biggest motors, and many parents give in.

The problem is that’s not how electric bikes work – there’s so much more to a bike than the motor wattage rating.

Motor design, controller current, battery voltage, thermal management, gearing, efficiency and software tuning all influence performance. A beautifully tuned 500W or 750W system can be far nicer to ride – and sometimes more useful – than a poorly implemented motor advertising twice the power.

But “excellent controller tuning” doesn’t look nearly as exciting in a giant font on an Amazon listing. So manufacturers respond rationally based on what consumers demand: They make the number bigger.

The result is an e-bike horsepower war that is ultimately hurting the entire industry.

When riders blast through bike paths on motorcycle-performance machines marketed as “e-bikes,” pedestrians don’t care whether the motor technically arrived in a street-legal mode. Police officers aren’t going to inspect controller settings. And lawmakers aren’t famous for approaching emerging transportation technology with surgical precision.

They see a fast machine with pedals, hear complaints about dangerous “e-bikes,” and start writing laws that affect everyone – including riders on perfectly ordinary commuter e-bikes.

In my opinion, that’s the part that should worry anyone who enjoys riding an e-bike.

Industry observers note that what we have is that essentially all of these things are mopeds (i.e. Class 3 at 40km/h) and not much like bicycles at all.

It isn't surprising that allowing people to ride around unregistered mopeds, often on infrastructure shared with pedestrians, has created a lot of strife.

Quite a lot of them are actually even more extreme than that, and really more like 125cc motorbikes.

There’s absolutely a place for high-powered electric two-wheelers. In fact, I want more of them. Lightweight electric mopeds and motorcycles could replace an enormous number of car trips while using a fraction of the energy and space. Those are highly capable machines, but they need to be used appropriately, registered legally, and ridden responsibly.

And we don’t help that cause by pretending they’re bicycles.

Perhaps the e-bike industry’s next great innovation doesn’t need another 500 watts.

It has been revealed that maybe it just needs a little more honesty about what we’re actually building. So let’s build more electric bicycles. And yes, let’s build more e-motos and electric motorcycles. But let’s not confuse the two, either.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1350 w)
