World’s fastest animal may gain habitat by 2080

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (455 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while climate change represents a threat to most animal populations, the reality isn’t quite as straight forward.
  • Industry observers note that that could be the case for peregrine falcons (Falco peregrinus), the fastest animal on the planet, living in the United Kingdom.
  • Panter analyzed how various future climate change scenarios might make different parts of the country more or less appropriate for 16 species of breeding birds of prey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while climate change represents a threat to most animal populations, the reality isn’t quite as straight forward. As the landscape reacts to a shifting climate, some species might actually see their habitat expand.

Industry observers note that that could be the case for peregrine falcons (Falco peregrinus), the fastest animal on the planet, living in the United Kingdom. That’s what Connor Panter, a researcher at the University of Nottingham’s School of Geography, found in a study published today in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.

Panter analyzed how various future climate change scenarios might make different parts of the country more or less appropriate for 16 species of breeding birds of prey.

“We know that climate change is altering where wildlife is found across the world, but scientists’ understanding of how different birds of prey may respond to these changes is still relatively limited,” Panter tells Popular Science. “Raptors play important ecological roles as predators, and understanding how their distributions might change is important for informing future conservation efforts.”.

It has been revealed that panter investigated a “middle-of-the-road” climate-change scenario and a “worst-case” climate-change scenario in the U.K. Today, there are 42,570 square miles of suitable habitat for peregrine falcons. Under the middle-of-the-road scenario, that could increase by 40.6 percent by 2060, and under the worst-case scenario, it could increase by 73.5 percent by 2080.

Hen harriers (Circus cyaneus), golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos), little owls (Athene noctua), long-eared owls (Asio otus), western barn owls (Tyto alba), and western marsh harriers (Circus aeruginosus) could also see increases. Suitable habitats for common buzzards (Buteo buteo), European sparrowhawks (Accipiter nisus), and tawny owls (Strix aluco), aren’t predicted to change much in any scenario. But British short-eared owls (Asio flammeus), red kites (Milvus milvus), merlins (Falco columbarius), and Eurasian goshawks (Astur gentilis) will likely lose significant amounts of suitable land.

Ultimately, Panter’s work emphasizes that climate change will probably not impact all birds of prey in the same way, even if they live in the same areas. This could represent a significant problem for conservation, because future efforts aiming to safeguard these species will have to take these differences into consideration, according to Panter.

Recent findings suggest that “It is also important to recognise that an increase in the area suitable for a species does not necessarily mean that its population will grow or that it will become more widespread,” Panter claims. For example, “whether peregrine falcons can occupy newly suitable areas will depend on numerous other factors, including the availability of prey, nesting opportunities, threats from humans and interactions with other species.”.

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

Industry observers note that according to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

It has been revealed that vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

It has been revealed that zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

Sources indicate that zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA said in a statement.

Sources indicate that “While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he indicated up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the classic Thanksgiving comedy Planes, Trains and Automobiles, hapless hero Del Griffith (played by the late, great John Candy) delivers an emotional riposte to Steve Martin’s uptight ad man Neal Page that stands as a beautifully dignified defense of kindness, empathy and self-love in the face of his own perceived shortcomings.

Recent findings suggest that “You want to hurt me? Go right ahead if it makes you feel any better…I could be a cold, hard cynic like you. But I don’t like to hurt people’s feelings. You think what you want about me, I’m not changing. I… I like me. My wife likes me…because I’m the real article. What you see is what you get.”.

For many of us around the holidays, particularly after a night of excess, Del and Neal’s exchange could read as our internal monologue – your kinder inner voice battling the internal bully who judges your every overindulgence. The jury’s out on whether the kind voice is ever as potent as Del’s is in that moment. But it should be, because when it comes to your health around the holidays, the bully has usually got it wrong.

Recent findings suggest that the truth is, for most of us, one day of immoderation during Thanksgiving is unlikely to matter in the grand scheme. As such, you would do well to avoid the litany of holiday season health myths out there, many of which seem hell-bent on punishing you for taking a day off:.

Like all misinformation, these kinds of medical myths are loud and tend to die hard, but they almost always trade on quick fixes that target the wrong thing.

In a recent development, A 2020 review of 23 observational studies found that most highlighted significant weight gain during festive periods, averaging roughly a pound and a half. One of the original studies, a landmark NIH study from 2000, found that much of that weight tends to stick around. So the question is not what you ate on Thanksgiving Thursday and how promptly you can “undo the damage,” but rather whether the extended holiday season becomes a two-month period where your healthy routine goes out the window. Some things to look out for on that front:.

None of this is a free pass for everyone. If you manage a health condition, you likely have less margin for error, even when talking about a single meal or a drink. Critical factors include timing, sodium intake, alcohol intake, and missed medication. A few non-exhaustive examples:.

Whatever condition you’re managing, the move for all of them remains the same – be prepared. Check your initiative with your care team before the holiday, not after, and call them if something feels off afterward.

Technically, feeling good on Black Friday starts on Thursday. A short and light walk after a feast can help smooth out post-meal blood sugar – the earlier the better, ideally within an hour of eating. Staying upright for a couple of hours to help with digestion, particularly if you’re prone to reflux, is also a great idea. If you’re on medication, remember to take it on time. And, at the risk of sounding prudish, and this goes for everyone: try to get to bed at a sensible hour.

Above all else, Thanksgiving is a holiday built around gratitude and kindness, so channel your inner Del Griffith and remember to be both grateful and kind, to yourself and to those around you – evidence suggests that’s also good for your health.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

According to recent reports, the first fully electric Porsche Boxster is finally in the home stretch of development. Ahead of its official debut in early 2027, Porsche offered an early look at the two-door electric sports car.

Despite rumors that the all-electric 718 Boxster was canceled, Porsche confirmed on Tuesday that the Boxster EV will debut in the first quarter of 2027.

“Starting next year, the all-electric 718 Boxster will offer our customers a compelling entry point into the world of two-door sports cars,” Porsche CEO Dr Michael Leiters said.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, Porsche is putting the electric sports car through the paces to ensure it preserves the DNA of its predecessors, a top priority.

Porsche developed a new “E-Core” architecture specifically for the 718 Boxster to lower the seat position and optimize weight distribution.

In a recent development, with the 800-volt battery mounted directly behind the seats, where the internal combustion engine would typically be found, the weight is concentrated toward the middle of the vehicle. The electric Boxster has a weight distribution of 40% on the front axle and 60% on the rear, matching that of a traditional mid-engined sports car.

It also features an “intelligent lightweight construction,” as Porsche calls it, so the vehicle’s overall weight matches that of the current 911 Cabriolet models with its T-Hybrid powertrain.

“Our engineers have succeeded in transferring the Boxster’s unique concept to the electric world, further enhancing it in the process,” Porsche’s CEO remarked.

It has been revealed that the electric Boxster shares many chassis components with the 911, including the steering, which is based on the 911 Carrera GTS. It will offer rear-axle steering, a first for the 718 Boxster.

Meanwhile, the wheel and tire dimensions and braking system are based on the Porsche 911, and the electronically controlled PTV+ limited-slip differential is also pulled from the 911.

Porsche mentioned the electric Boxster will be “the most powerful 718 ever,” but didn’t offer a specific output figure.

The range-topping Boxster EV can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under three seconds, according to Porsche, and it can reach a top speed of over 155 mph (250 km/h).

According to recent reports, all electric Boxster models will be RWD and come standard with E-Shift. Like Hyundai’s performance N EVs, including the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, the Porsche Boxster EV features a virtual gear shift that simulates the feeling and sounds of a seven-speed PDK transmission.

When E-Shift mode is not active, the paddle can be used to toggle between three levels of recuperation.

The electric Porsche 718 Boxster will make its official debut in the first quarter of 2027, so we should learn more details soon. IT will be built at Porsche’s main plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen, Germany.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that lucid has its sights set on America’s burgeoning autonomous-vehicle ecosystem, and now it's one notable step closer to getting robotaxis on the road. The California electric vehicle startup, along with Uber and self-driving technology manufacturer Nuro, has started testing driverless Gravity SUVs in the San Francisco Bay Area, the companies announced Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that more than 100 Gravitys have already been testing on public roads in San Francisco and Houston since January, but every one of them had a human supervisor in the driver's seat. Taking the safety operator out of the vehicle is a major step ahead of the service's planned commercial launch in the Bay Area in the first quarter of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the stakes are high for Lucid. The luxury automaker has burned through billions and struggled to meaningfully scale up its vehicle sales of the Air and Gravity. Increasingly, it's turning to the growing robotaxi market for a upcoming source of sales volume and revenue. It plans to deploy tens of thousands of robotaxis in the U.S. and Europe.

Sources indicate that if things go to plan, Lucid, Uber, and Nuro will join Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox as the few companies offering truly driverless paid ride-hailing in the U.S. Unlike those rivals, which offer rides through their own dedicated apps, the Gravity will be available through Uber. Uber has set out to become the go-to platform for driverless vehicles, and has struck deals to put Waymo and Zoox taxis on its app in certain cities. Uber's exclusivity deal with Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, however, will end in 2028 as the Alphabet-owned tech giant plans to shift to its own app in those cities.

According to recent reports, lucid said initial phase of on-road driverless testing will take place in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale. More Bay Area cities will be added next year. A fleet of more than 100 Gravitys are included in these driverless tests, all of which have hardware and software upgrades compared to those in the previous phase of testing.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, the Gravity has some advantages over its competitors. It is among the longest-range and fastest-charging electric SUVs in the U.S., with up to 450 miles of range on a single charge and 400-kilowatt charging that can add 200 miles in as little as 11 minutes. That should mean fewer charging stops and less downtime, which could potentially keep the vehicle earning fares for longer.

Lucid Gravity robotaxi commercial roadmap.

Recent findings suggest that it will also have to maintain a high utilization rate to recover its steep starting price, which begins at $81,750 for the passenger version without any autonomous hardware and software. (Lucid hasn’t said how much the robotaxi version costs, or how much the extra weight affects range and efficiency.).

The Gravity isn’t Lucid’s only vehicle that will someday do robotaxi duty. The upcoming midsize platform will also spawn a robotaxi, although Lucid hasn’t mentioned if it will be a version of the Cosmos or something else entirely.

#224332. Industry News: Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2083 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.
  • Industry observers note that amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just launched its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim.
  • According to recent reports, both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.

Industry observers note that amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just launched its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim. Meanwhile, ALSO, the high-tech electric bicycle startup spun out of Rivian, revealed that it was halting deliveries of its futuristic TM-B electric bicycle amid mounting software problems.

According to recent reports, both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical. Both have deep engineering roots and were incubated by successful technology companies. And both have developed impressive proprietary systems that set their bikes apart from the competition.

But their dramatically different rolls out offer an interesting lesson about the difference between innovation and execution, and which has proven to be more successful in the real world.

Amflow’s story actually begins before the brand launched its first electric mountain bike.

In a recent development, DJI, the Chinese drone giant, had spent years perfecting the art of building small, lightweight, powerful electric motors, sophisticated electronic controllers, and advanced battery management systems. Those are all technologies that translate remarkably well to electric bicycles, even if the applications are quite different.

Industry observers note that that expertise helped give rise to the Avinox e-bike drive system, which quickly earned a reputation as one of the most impressive electric bicycle drivetrains on the market. The mid-drive motor and control system rapidly ate away at the huge market share long held by Bosch and other leaders.

The motors offered an almost ridiculous amount of power in a lightweight package, paired with sophisticated sensors and software that delivered smooth, natural-feeling pedal assistance. The system was also designed as a tightly integrated ecosystem, with displays, controllers, batteries, and motors working together.

Amflow’s first electric mountain bikes demonstrated just how well that technology could work in the real world.

And now, with the launch of the fresh Amflow UE commuter series, the manufacturer is taking that proven technology and applying it to an entirely different kind of riding.

The new bikes bring Avinox’s powerful pedal assistance and intelligent electronic controls to a more practical urban platform, adding commuter-focused features designed to make everyday riding more convenient.

There’s plenty of proprietary technology here, but perhaps the most key thing about Amflow’s approach is what the company didn’t reinvent.

The bikes still fundamentally work like bicycles.

According to recent reports, you pedal, a conventional mechanical drivetrain transfers that power to the rear wheel, and an electric motor provides assistance. It’s the same basic arrangement that has worked on electric bicycles for decades, just refined with much more advanced engineering.

Recent findings suggest that amflow didn’t need to fundamentally change the bicycle to make it feel futuristic. Instead, the firm focused on making the familiar bicycle experience better.

Sources indicate that and while the new commuter models are still too fresh to judge their long-term reliability, early impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. That’s an encouraging start, especially considering the manufacturer’s already established reputation in the demanding electric mountain bike market.

ALSO, on the other hand, took a dramatically different approach.

The organization emerged from Rivian, the American electric vehicle manufacturer known for its technologically advanced electric trucks and SUVs.

Sources indicate that like DJI, Rivian has extensive experience developing sophisticated electric drivetrains, battery systems, power electronics, and software. And like Amflow, ALSO wanted to bring that expertise to a newly introduced generation of electric bicycles.

But instead of using those technologies to improve a conventional bicycle, ALSO decided to rethink the entire machine.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer’s TM-B electric bicycle uses a pedal-by-wire system, meaning the pedals aren’t mechanically connected to the rear wheel. Instead, pedaling turns a generator that sends data signals and power through an electronic system, while software determines how the rear motor responds.

Pedal-by-wire systems have some genuine potential advantages. They can eliminate traditional chains, belts, derailleurs, and other mechanical drivetrain components, which has helped land them on many unconventional e-bikes such as extremely long cargo e-bikes and truck-like electric bicycles that would otherwise require ridiculously long chain runs.

They can also allow engineers to completely customize the relationship between pedaling effort and motor response, creating riding experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a conventional bicycle drivetrain.

But there’s a catch. When you replace a relatively simple mechanical system with a sophisticated electronic one, you’re also introducing a lot more opportunities for things to go wrong.

And unlike a conventional bicycle, where many drivetrain problems can be diagnosed and repaired with basic tools, a highly proprietary software-defined bicycle can become much more dependent on its manufacturer to keep it running.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not inherently a bad tradeoff. Modern electric cars have demonstrated that software-defined vehicles can offer tremendous benefits. But it puts enormous pressure on the manufacturer to get the hardware, software, and integration right.

Unfortunately, ALSO’s early rollout suggests that the company hasn’t quite managed that yet.

The contrast between the two companies became particularly striking last week.

Amflow unveiled its latest commuter models, building on the reputation of its successful electric mountain bikes and earning enthusiastic early reviews.

Recent findings suggest that ALSO, meanwhile, confirmed that it was pausing deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycle due to software-related issues. That’s on top of earlier delivery delays and reports of customers having to send their latest ALSO TM-B bicycles back for repairs.

We’ve also previously reported on some unusual charging and discharging behavior with the TM-B, raising questions about how the bike’s sophisticated electronic systems were managing energy. Those concerns now look particularly relevant in light of the tech giant’s latest announcement.

To be fair, we don’t know how widespread the problems are across ALSO’s delivered bicycles, and it’s entirely possible that the company will resolve these complications relatively rapidly with updates on delivered bikes and reflashing software on bikes yet to be shipped.

It has been revealed that nor should we assume that Amflow’s latest commuter bikes will be trouble-free simply because their initial reviews are positive. Long-term reliability is something that can only be established over time. But the difference in their respective launches is hard to ignore.

Both are examples of tech-focused startups attempting to reinvent the future of e-bikes. One tech giant is expanding its lineup after successfully establishing its technology in the market. The other is struggling to get its first product consistently into customers’ hands.

And that brings us to what I think is the most interesting part of this story.

There’s a fundamental difference between developing impressive technology and successfully turning that technology into a dependable consumer product.

Both Amflow and ALSO have accomplished the first part.

The engineering behind the Avinox drive system is genuinely impressive, and the TM-B’s pedal-by-wire architecture is one of the more ambitious attempts to rethink the electric bicycle in recent years.

But Amflow appears to have taken a more measured approach to bringing that technology to consumers.

The manufacturer first developed and refined a sophisticated electric bicycle drivetrain, proved it in the demanding electric mountain bike market, and then adapted it to commuter applications.

ALSO attempted something much more ambitious right out of the gate: launching an entirely fresh bicycle architecture with numerous interdependent proprietary systems.

According to recent reports, neither approach is inherently wrong. In fact, if nobody ever attempted the latter, we’d probably miss out on some genuinely revolutionary products. But there’s a reason that so many successful technological innovations are evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes the smartest engineering decision isn’t figuring out how to replace something that already works. It’s figuring out how to make it work better.

And there’s a certain irony in the fact that Amflow’s new commuter bike looks relatively ordinary, yet appears to deliver an extraordinary riding experience.

ALSO’s TM-B, meanwhile, looks like something from the future, but its early ownership experience has been considerably less impressive.

I want to be clear that I’m not rooting for or against either company here.

It has been revealed that quite the opposite. Both ALSO and Amflow are working to accelerate the state of the industry. I’ve been fascinated by the TM-B since it was first unveiled, and I genuinely hope the organization succeeds. And Amflow has taken the fresh perspective brought by its parent company, DJI, and turned it into real-world progress. The e-bike industry needs more innovation to help push everyone forward.

I love seeing companies take massive swings in the electric bicycle industry, especially when they’re attempting something more interesting than slapping a bigger motor and battery onto an otherwise generic frame.

And I think pedal-by-wire technology has real potential. The ability to electronically control the relationship between pedaling and propulsion opens up fascinating possibilities, even if it also introduces latest challenges.

I should also mention that I have not personally ridden either of these bikes, and thus this is analysis from the sidelines. The Amflow UE Carbon was only unveiled a few days ago, though I’ve got one on the way and am excited to begin testing it soon and to report back here on the experience. As for ALSO, the bike was unveiled a year ago, and I was slated to be at the launch for test riding, but barely an hour after I posted an exclusive article revealing that ALSO had accidentally leaked its own images of its yet-to-be-unveiled bike on its website, I received an email uninviting me to the upcoming event and test ride.

So keep in mind that all of this is being remarked as an analyst with nearly two decades in the e-bike industry and hundreds of different e-bikes under my belt, not from personal experience with either bike model.

Industry observers note that but as someone who spends an enormous amount of time riding, testing, and working on electric bicycles, I also appreciate the value of simplicity. A bicycle is an inherently elegant machine. It’s lightweight, efficient, relatively easy to maintain, and remarkably dependable considering how few components it needs to function.

Electric assistance has already made that machine dramatically more useful for millions of people. The question is how much more complexity we should introduce in pursuit of further improvements.

Amflow seems to be asking, “How can we use advanced technology to make riding a bicycle better?”.

ALSO seems to be asking, “What if we could completely rethink how a bicycle works?”.

Both are worthwhile questions, and I’m glad there are companies pursuing both answers. But right now, Amflow is demonstrating the advantages of building on a proven foundation, while ALSO is learning some painful lessons about the challenges of reinventing the wheel.

Sources indicate that it's pretty clear that electric cars are much simpler than ICE cars, and I would argue this is an advantage. However, the same cannot be noted for the ALSO bike. It's much more complicated than a normal bike, or even a normal e-bike. It seems like an answer in search of a problem.

And perhaps that’s the biggest takeaway from this tale of two high-tech e-bike startups.

It has been revealed that the future of electric bicycles will undoubtedly involve more sophisticated motors, batteries, sensors, and software. But the companies that succeed won’t necessarily be the ones that pack the most technology into their bikes.

They’ll be the ones that figure out how to make all that technology work so seamlessly that riders barely have to think about it.

According to recent reports, because at the end of the day, the best electric bicycle isn’t necessarily the one with the most advanced technology. It’s the one that makes you want to ride it every day – and actually lets you.

The Improbable Success of a ‘Poky Little Motoring Show’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, through the lens of time, the early part of the Aughts can seem like a simpler age when phones were usually dumb, politicians were sometimes smart, and families gathered quaintly around one TV set to watch the same program at the same time.
  • This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.
  • In a recent development, in fact, Top Gear predated this century, debuting on BBC television in 1977 and plodding through the Eighties and Nineties with sensible car-buying advice and cozy trips to steam rallies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, through the lens of time, the early part of the Aughts can seem like a simpler age when phones were usually dumb, politicians were sometimes smart, and families gathered quaintly around one TV set to watch the same program at the same time. High-resolution internet video and the streaming revolution were distant spots on the horizon. But the changing landscape unwittingly created the perfect conditions for an accidental phenomenon: a TV show about cars with an estimated global audience of 350 million, a broadcasting triumph that would be impossible to replicate today. Because the Aughts was the decade that seeded the improbable success of a self-confessed “poky little motoring show” called Top Gear.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

In a recent development, in fact, Top Gear predated this century, debuting on BBC television in 1977 and plodding through the Eighties and Nineties with sensible car-buying advice and cozy trips to steam rallies. The series added Jeremy Clarkson to its hosting lineup in 1988 to bring a bit of wit to what was still a fundamentally earnest format. In 1999, he left the show, and two years later, the BBC declared that Top Gear was going to be “rested,” a polite British way of saying “canceled.”.

At the same time, Jeremy and an old school friend, TV producer Andy Wilman, who had been a lesser Top Gear presenter, were working on plans for a bigger, more boisterous car show called Carmageddon. When the pair pitched it to the head of the BBC Two channel, she liked the idea and agreed to commission the show with one proviso: Carmageddon should become a reboot of Top Gear. The fuse had been lit, but free­wheeling global success wasn’t the master strategy. In fact, there was no grand scheme, only a vague hope to make a halfway-­decent show for audiences in the U.K. I know this because from 2002 to 2015, I was Top Gear’s script editor.

Industry observers note that this, like so much of the show, was something of an accident. I’d worked briefly with Jeremy on the old version of Top Gear, and he’d liked my satirical car website, Sniff Petrol, but if I hadn’t bumped into him in a restaurant and been invited to “come in for a chat,” perhaps the opportunity would have passed me by. As it is, I went to see Jeremy and Andy, and I listened to their ideas, many of which sounded strange. A racing driver who couldn’t tell you anything about a car because he never spoke? A segment forcing celebrities to drive around a track in a low-budget grocery getter? An indoor studio for a car show? Hmm. But Jeremy and Andy are persuasive people, and I agreed to join nonetheless.

We auditioned a lot of people to co-host and eventually found Richard Hammond, a car journalist who performed an unremarkable screen test but then reduced us to hysterics with self-deprecating stories as he was walking toward the exit.

We made a pilot episode, which was a disaster, then a second pilot episode, which was also a disaster, after which point there was no time to try again because we had a scheduled on-air date. We’d go to the pub after work and sit there making despairing sighs and ask, “What are we doing?” We were not plotting world domination. Our biggest goal was to get a show out on time so the BBC didn’t have to broadcast reruns instead.

But we were allowed to carry on, and our first season attracted modest viewing figures, just passing the low target the BBC had issued. Back then, some broadcasters were willing to nurture shows and let them grow gently rather than demanding instant success.

In a recent development, top Gear needed this patience because it often felt like we were making it up as we went along. In the popular consciousness, the show is remembered for Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, and James May driving malfunctioning cars across harsh and distant lands. But it didn’t start like that at all. We didn’t have James in season one (BBC management thought he was too similar to Jeremy); instead, a car dealer called Jason Dawe was in the third spot. We didn’t go abroad because we were a British show and thought we should film in the U.K., no matter how gray and rainy it might be. We didn’t put the three hosts together in the field until the fourth season, an experiment that yielded nuggets of gold. We never planned to create epic road trips occupying entire shows, until a journey across the Southern United States generated too much material to squeeze into a 20-minute film and was allowed to roam free as an hour-long special.

What we did have from the start was a certain editorial rigor. Jeremy began his career as a local newspaper journalist. Richard had a background in live radio. James worked on car magazines for years. They’d grown up in worlds that demanded quick thinking and an endless supply of ideas. Sometimes Jeremy would stride into the office booming, “I’ve had a thought . . . .” Sometimes we’d sit around, batting stupid notions back and forth.

Industry observers note that as part of my job, I’d scribble down what we noted, then try to hack the best bits into something workable. After that came the notable part. Any idea, no matter how brilliant it first seemed, was then poked and prodded and dismantled to make sure it was as good as it could be. When we had a full episode’s worth of vetted ideas, I’d sit down with one or all of the presenters, and we’d write a script. For a solo track test, this would be detailed and extensive. For a three-header out in the field, the introduction would be tightly written to make sure our mission was clear, in our minds and to the viewers, after which there would be rough scene headings and perhaps the odd one-liner. As a production team, we’d proposal situations and challenges that we thought would allow the hosts to run free with ad-libs and arguing.

Sources indicate that jeremy, Richard, and James were very different people with a love of cars as their common ground. We never had to fake their on-screen personalities; that’s just who they were. Jeremy, bombastic and attention seeking. Richard, excitable and a verbal sniper with killer one-­liners. James, often giving the impression that he’d rather be at home dis­mantling a motorcycle than forced to hang out with these two morons. The dynamic worked.

That such a poorly planned piece of programming eventually found itself a global success is down to the decade in which it was born, a time when people still watched the same show at the same time. One inadvertent stroke of genius was the BBC’s decision to schedule Top Gear on a Sunday evening, traditionally a quiet night on TV in the U.K. Among straight-faced detective shows and florid costume dramas, the hijinks of Top Gear—a nun in a monster truck, a bus jumping motorcycles, a man trying to destroy a To­yota Hilux in increasingly elaborate ways—shone like a beacon of eccentricity. The next morning, everyone could go into work or school and talk about it.

Industry observers note that ratings grew steadily. Then, during filming in 2006 for the ninth season, Richard crashed a jet-­propelled dragster. The show was paused while he recovered from serious injuries. When we returned, viewing figures in the U.K. jumped dramatically.

According to recent reports, global success came later, especially with the growth of YouTube and other social media. ­Suddenly anyone could clip out their favorite bits of Top Gear and make them accessible all around the world. An American gearhead called Alex Mills founded a site called FinalGear, where fans could discuss Top Gear and share BitTorrent links so people everywhere could download the show, if not entirely legally. Top Gear became cult viewing in countries where car indicates weren’t trying to turn pickup trucks into boats and a three-wheeled car into a space shuttle. Which was, of course, everywhere else.

Also, the car landscape of the Aughts gave the show great material upon which to build. It was the era of the hypercar, and at its peak was that stats-heavy poster child, the Bugatti Veyron. But it was also a time when Subaru and Mitsubishi were slugging it out to make the best roadgoing rally car. Countless manufacturers were serving up everything from high-powered wagons to hyperactive hot hatches. Best of all, in the U.K. at least, secondhand cars were fantastically cheap and accessible, even old supercars.

It has been revealed that at the time, living hand to mouth simply trying to get the show done, we didn’t realize how lucky we were, though I hope we made the most of the luck that came our way. The reports of ever-­bigger audiences seemed abstract and unbelievable. Only when it became harder and harder to find any country in the world where our filming presence wouldn’t attract a large and excitable crowd did we start to realize that perhaps this stupid show of ours was catching on.

According to recent reports, nonetheless, we rarely had time to rest on our laurels. Indeed, Andy Wilman actively tried to stop us from becoming full of ourselves by, among other things, stridently discouraging attempts to make our disgustingly shabby offices nicer. He believed we had a job to do, and that job was to make an hour of entertainment for Sunday nights on BBC television. The rest was an implausible-­sounding bonus. And perhaps by dint of not trying too hard to be globally appealing, Top Gear became a worldwide phenomenon of the Aughts and beyond. It really couldn’t have happened at any other time.

Every Brand Selling Hybrid Vehicles in the U.S. for 2027

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For all the talk about electric vehicles over the past several years, the bigger story is the current hybrid wave.
  • This means that there’s now more choice than ever among hybrid vehicles: nearly every major automaker offers at least one hybrid model, and many of them offer a wide range of hybrids in various body styles from SUVs to sports cars and everything in between.
  • Every Brand Selling Sports Cars | Every Brand Selling EVs | Best-Looking Cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For all the talk about electric vehicles over the past several years, the bigger story is the current hybrid wave. From 2024 until the end of September 2026, gas-electric hybrids soared from just over eight percent of upcoming light-duty vehicle sales to 16 percent, or double the share of EVs, according to the Energy Information Administration. After consecutive years of parallel growth that saw battery-electric and gas-electric vehicles rise together starting in 2020, hybrid sales have never been higher while EVs, despite a spurt in 2025 and 2026, are not recovering.

This means that there’s now more choice than ever among hybrid vehicles: nearly every major automaker offers at least one hybrid model, and many of them offer a wide range of hybrids in various body styles from SUVs to sports cars and everything in between. Here’s a guide to all hybrids on sale, across all segments (excluding 48-volt hybrids that are not designed to power a vehicle solely with electric motors).

Every Brand Selling Sports Cars | Every Brand Selling EVs | Best-Looking Cars.

Industry observers note that bentley makes the world’s only four-seat plug-in hybrid convertible, the Continental GTC. The ravishing powertrain, standard with 671 horsepower or 771 horsepower in the Speed and Mulliner, isn’t exclusive to the the Continental range, either. The twin-turbo V-8 and its 22-kWh battery pack are shared with the Flying Spur sedan, both of which claim 30 miles of electric range (we did 49 in the Continental). A turbo V-6 and an 18-kWh battery are found in the Bentayga Hybrid SUV.

BMW offers a sextet of plug-in hybrids that throw heavy punches under hard acceleration. The 550e, 750e, and X5 xDrive50e share a 483-hp setup with a turbo inline-six good for between 34 and 44 miles of electric range, while the M5, M5 Touring and XM electrify a twin-turbo V-8 for a total of 717 or 738 horsepower. We expect to see more hybrid setups on the high-performance end of the lineup in the future, although the next-gen M3 is also offering a fully electric variant, signifying a possible shift in BMW’s strategy.

Chevrolet’s sole hybrids are found within the Corvette lineup. The first is the Grand Sport X, which supplements the base Stingray’s 6.7-liter V-8 with a front electric motor for a total of 721 horsepower. The other is the ZR1X, which costs a quarter-million dollars and pumps 1250 horsepower from a turbo 5.5-liter V-8 and a front electric motor. It gets 12 mpg in the city and goes 225 mph. It’s beyond magnificent. Still, Chevy is planning more mainstream hybrids, as the three-row Traverse SUV is poised to get a hybrid variant in the future.

It has been revealed that all mid-engine Ferraris come as hybrids—and 869 horsepower is the bare minimum. That’s the output from the twin-turbo flat-plane V-6 and axial-flux motor in the fresh 296 Speciale. The wedgy 849 Testarossa stuffs a twin-turbo V-8 and triple motors for 1036 horsepower. For $3.7 million, the almighty F80 goes backward in cylinder count (but with a more powerful twin-turbo V-6 and three motors) and forward with F1 tech for 1184 horsepower. Buy a front-engine Ferrari and you’ll have to settle for nonhybrid V-12s and V-8s.

Industry observers note that ford sold some of the industry’s first PHEVs in the 2010s—remember the Fusion Energi?—but no longer offers any hybrid sedans or SUVs. The Escape Hybrid and PHEV are gone. But one of our favorite hybrids on sale is the Maverick compact pickup, which can hit 40-plus mpg in the city with front- or all-wheel drive. The F-150 PowerBoost, which uses a twin-turbo V-6 with an electric motor, is more capable but not as smooth to drive as the Maverick.

The first Genesis hybrids aren’t launching until the 2028 model year in the U.S., but we decided to include them here anyway. The lineup includes the gorgeous G80 mid-size luxury sedan and the stately GV80 mid-size luxury SUV. Their hybrid powertrains both use turbo 2.5-liter inline-fours and represent the next stage of the Hyundai group’s hybrid expertise. The batteries now use liquid instead of air cooling, a seven-speed automatic replaces the six-speed, and the torque output (391 lb-ft) matches the twin-turbo V-6 in the 3.5T trims.

According to recent reports, honda has been into hybrids almost as long as Toyota has (see the 1999 Honda Insight), and the company’s current hybrid powertrain is a gem. With direct drive (no transmission), the two-motor, 2.0-liter inline-four setup is quick, efficient, and downright fun. It’s available on the CR-V, the Civic sedan and hatchback, and the Accord sedan, and it’s the only choice on the Prelude coupe.

According to recent reports, while the Elantra Hybrid takes a hiatus until 2028, Hyundai’s next-best mileage champ is the Sonata Hybrid, which can surpass 50 mpg and offers generous rear leg room. Hyundai’s three compact and mid-size SUVs, including a upcoming-gen Tucson, get hybrid versions and all offer all-wheel drive. Unlike many mainstream hybrids, Hyundai employs a six-speed automatic instead of a CVT or direct drive. The Tucson plug-in hybrid is no longer available.

According to recent reports, while Jeep axed the plug-in hybrid 4xe trims of the Wrangler and Grand Cherokee, an extended-range series hybrid is coming to the Grand Wagoneer with a whopping 647 horsepower. The hybrid-only Cherokee compact SUV comes with only 210 horsepower but up to an estimated 39 mpg city rating.

Sources indicate that like Hyundai, Kia’s diversity of gas, hybrid, and electric powertrains has paid off in spades in terms of sales. There are eight hybrids total in the Kia lineup, with plug-in hybrids available on the Sorento and Sportage (no longer on the Niro). Every SUV has a hybrid option, and so does the Carnival minivan.

Sources indicate that surprised to see Lamborghini peddling hybrids? The brand’s lineup is now entirely hybrid, actually, starting with the plug-in hybrid Urus SUV which comes in 789-hp SE and 801-hp Performante versions. Those SUVs can do an estimated 35 miles on electricity. The 907-hp Temerario is also a plug-in hybrid, offering a pitiful four miles of electric range. But the only hybrid that revs to 10,000 rpm. Then there’s the 1001-hp Revuelto and 1050-hp Revuelto SV which pair a giant V-12 with three electric motors. What a time to be alive.

According to recent reports, leave it to Lexus to combine massive power with efficiency. This was the brand that in 2008 gave us the LS600hL, a hybrid flagship that could match the refinement from 12-cylinder German sedans. Now that we live in an SUV world, the LX700h is the modern equivalent—at up to $143,000, it’s the rare four-passenger hybrid SUV with four-wheel drive and a fully reclining rear seat. The TX500h is the next step down (the PHEV is gone for 2027). The RX and NX each offer three hybrid trims including plug-ins, while the latest ES350h is now the sole hybrid sedan.

Industry observers note that lincoln moved away from hybrids only to come running back—and they took a long way home. The brand’s two hybrid SUVs, the compact Corsair and mid-size two-row Nautilus, are plucked straight from China, since Ford hasn’t yet carved out factory space for these models in North America. They enjoy a substantial exterior refresh for 2027, too. Each comes with turbo inline-fours and all-wheel drive, while the Nautilus goes screen crazy with a 48-inch display hugging the bottom of the windshield.

While the CX-50 Hybrid uses a Toyota-based powertrain, the CX-90 Hybrid is all Mazda. It’s a nicely styled three-row plug-in hybrid SUV with an estimated 25 miles of electric range. The two-row CX-70 Hybrid is discontinued, but there’s a CX-5 Hybrid on the horizon, though it may not arrive until 2028.

Want a Le Mans racer as a comfortable supercar? There’s no better choice than a McLaren Artura, which has a howling twin-turbo V-6 that has the party trick of leaving and arriving in complete silence. With 11 miles of estimated electric range, it can go nearly three times as far on a charge than a Lamborghini Temerario can. The combined 690 horsepower and McLaren’s light-as-a-feather chassis are heavenly. Choose the coupe or a spider.

According to recent reports, while AMG customers weren’t so enthusiastic about the C63 and its F1-derived four-cylinder plug-in hybrid powertrain, they’re happy plugging into turbo-sixes and turbo V-8s on the higher-end models. Every hybrid AMG is PHEV, whether it’s a sedan, wagon, SUV, convertible, or coupe. The E Performance trims of the SL and GT Coupe make more than 1000 pound-feet of torque.

In a recent development, mercedes-Benz’s three hybrid models are all plug-in hybrids just like their AMG cousins, only less potent. The S580e is our personal favorite, as we were able to reach 58 miles of all-electric range on the highway, handily beating the factory estimate. The GLE500e also shares the same inline-six and delivers similar range, while the GLC350e has an inline-four. Like the AMGs, the GLE and S-class hybrids support DC fast charging, a rare feature on a PHEV.

According to recent reports, mitsubishi was first to market with a plug-in SUV, and it hasn’t really received due credit. Part of it is the premium price the Outlander PHEV commands and its so-so performance, though it’s updated for 2027 with more power. It also has plenty of features, decent interior quality, and a healthy 45-mile electric range. Along with the regular Outlander, it’s also the only three-row SUV in the compact segment.

It has been revealed that as the only series hybrid in the mainstream segment, Nissan has made a big splash with the Rogue Hybrid after more than a decade without any gas-electric powertrain in its lineup. Think of the tech giant’s e-Power hybrid setup like an extended-range EV where the gas engine serves only as a generator for the electric motors, but without the plug or the big battery. We like how it drives—a lot.

In a recent development, porsche’s conventional hybrid powertrain sits in its most prized product, the 911, where the T-Hybrid installs one or two electric turbos and a small battery on the GTS and Turbo S. The models with the E-Hybrid badge are plug-in hybrids. The Panamera has three PHEV choices, including the Turbo’s V-8 powertrain shared with Bentley for up to 771 horsepower. The Cayenne Hybrid has either a V-6 hybrid setup or a similar V-8 setup in either the SUV or Coupe body style.

Panamera Turbo E-Hybrid / S Turbo E-Hybrid.

According to recent reports, throne of Eros also doubles as the fresh Wish Pool, which is the one that has all of the game’s love interests in a single banner. This is a limited-time affair, of course, but it’s not the only thing you should look forward to here.

The even bigger news is that you can target your Wishes through the Xspace Echo, which lets you select five Memories to create your own pool from. You can use this to get any Memories you might not have, of course.

On the topic of Memories, you’ll also be able to unlock fresh second anniversary KV Memories, as part of a Yearly Highlights Event that will let you look back on your own journey with the game over the past year.

On the story and narrative side, Throne of Eros adds two latest main stories, with new branches for Xavier, and Rafayel. There’s even a narrative-specific event that will run throughout the anniversary period, through which you can earn two daily outfits for each of the five love interests.

Sources indicate that the celebrations also extend to upcoming anniversary content like mail, and video calls. You can purchase a Yearly Pass, and check out some new arrivals at the Lunar Shop.

Beyond the anniversary content, version 5.0 also adds a new feature to the game: Home, which essentially offers a hub to get you directly to interacting with love interests that doesn’t have to do with combat or story.

You can also expect various other quality of life updates that touch on the Journal, Phone Moments Search, Resources Quick Cleanup, and newly introduced Tete-a-Tete that should make interacting with all of them more streamlined.

It has been revealed that while this is a special banner, you should brush up on how banners work in Love and Deepspace if you’re unfamiliar. As always, it’s never not a good idea to check our Love and Deepspace codes page for some freebies.

Two-Thirds of Dementia Content On TikTok Is Misleading, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh survey suggests that about two-thirds of dementia advice videos on TikTok are misleading.

Of the videos examined, the analysis shows that nearly half contained inaccurate and potentially damaging information.

The researchers say that approximately 44% of TikTok creators who share dementia content lack credibility and appropriate qualifications.

Although misleading dementia content may appear on other social media platforms, this research examined only TikTok content, warranting further investigation.

The survey was commissioned by Homewatch Caregivers and has not been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

A spokesperson for TikTok told Healthline that if health-related content is potentially harmful, it is flagged for removal. The spokesperson added that 99.6% of misinformation deemed violative was proactively removed from the platform in 2026.

The spokesperson added that TikTok relies on fact-checking and guidance from public health authorities to help assess the accuracy of content. The platform may also apply warning labels to content that cannot be verified as accurate.

Looking to social media for health information is not uncommon. A recent poll reports that 31% of adults in the United States use social media at least once a month to look for health information and advice.

Experts advise seeking information about dementia from trusted sources, such as a primary care doctor and organizations like the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and the Alzheimer’s Association, rather than social media, where content creators who share advice often lack expertise.

“It’s normal to want answers quickly when you’re caring for someone living with dementia, and a short video from someone who seems to know what they’re talking about can be really convincing,” said lead researcher Jennifer Winarski, senior manager of care operations and quality for Homewatch CareGivers.

Sources indicate that “Despite there being some genuinely helpful information out there, you don’t always know whether it’s backed by medical evidence, so we wanted to bring our own expertise to uncover whether popular TikToks can be trusted,” she told Healthline. “We hope our report will encourage people to be a bit more careful about what they act on.”.

For the survey, researchers selected a sample of 500 of the most-watched dementia-related videos on TikTok with hashtags such as:.

Researchers then transcribed the video data to assess its accuracy.

In a recent development, the researchers found that two-thirds (66.4%) of the popular TikTok videos contained misleading information. Of those videos, about half (47.6%) contained potentially damaging misleading dementia information.

“It’s clear that many of the creators mean well, but much of what we saw was personal opinion rather than proven information, and in a few cases, general good health tips were presented as if they were specifically helpful for individuals living with dementia,” Winarski said.

“If families act on that, they could end up spending time and money on things that won’t help — and in the worst of cases, it could delay getting the support their loved one really needs,” she added.

Dung Trinh, MD, an internist for MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of the Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, noted it’s notable to be aware of the volume of misleading dementia information on social media. Trinh was not involved in this survey.

Some people may be making decisions about their health based on incomplete, misleading, or incorrect information, he mentioned.

“For example, someone might see a video claiming that a particular supplement can reverse Alzheimer’s disease or that certain memory problems automatically mean someone has dementia,” Trinh stated.

“These messages can lead to unnecessary fear, false reassurance, wasted money, or delays in getting a proper diagnosis.”.

“We are entering an exciting era in Alzheimer’s care, with advances in blood-based biomarkers, earlier detection, and treatments that may slow disease progression in appropriately selected patients,” Trinh continued.

“Getting an accurate diagnosis and receiving timely medical guidance are becoming increasingly crucial.”.

It has been revealed that the researchers examined the content creators behind the TikTok videos included in their analysis. They found that 44% of video creators behind the misleading videos had no relevant qualifications.

Rehan Aziz, MD, vice chair of education in the Department of Psychiatry at Hackensack Meridian Jersey Shore University Medical Center and associate professor of psychiatry and neurology at the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine in Fresh Jersey, said that content creators offering dementia advice should have relevant qualifications. Aziz wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Start by looking at the creator’s profile for a full name and a specific credential, such as MD, DO, PhD, or RN, along with a specialty,” Aziz told Healthline.

“For dementia, the most relevant experts include neurologists, geriatric psychiatrists, geriatricians, neuropsychologists, and nurses, including advanced practice nurses, or social workers who specialize in dementia care.”.

“You can confirm a doctor’s license through your state’s licensing board website and check board certification at certificationmatters.org,” Aziz said.

Sources indicate that as of 2020, more than 55 million people worldwide were living with dementia — a neurological condition that negatively affects the brain. Researchers predict this number will hit 78 million by 2030.

The increase in the number of people seeking dementia content online is a reflection of this trend.

When looking for accurate dementia information and guidance, Nestor Beltre, MD, a neurologist with Baptist Health Kenneth C. Griffin Neuroscience Institute, part of Baptist Health South Florida, noted a great first step is to speak with their primary care physician. Beltre wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Memory changes can occur for many different reasons, and some causes, including vitamin deficiencies, depression, and certain medical conditions, may be treatable,” he told Healthline.

According to recent reports, “Early evaluation can help identify what may be contributing to these changes and determine the most appropriate next steps. Depending on the individual’s symptoms, a neurologist, psychiatrist, or neuropsychologist can provide further evaluation and guidance,” Belter continued.

Beltre advised turning to trusted resources such as the Alzheimer’s Association and the National Institute on Aging, which can increase public understanding of memory-related conditions and available treatment options.

“The most notable message is that patients and families have resources available to help them better understand and manage cognitive health,” he mentioned.

#224327. Breaking: Meteorites fascinated ancient Egyptians—just look at King Tut’s ‘space dagger’

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1345 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Meteorites fascinated ancient Egyptians—just look at King Tut’s ‘space dagger’

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In August 2026, an analysis of iron from ancient Greek tombs revealed surprising results.
  • It seems that, among the upper classes of Bronze Age Greece, rings fashioned from this out-of-this-world metal were all the rage.
  • Researchers believe that the Greek meteoric rings were actually imported from Egypt: a land with a special relationship to this metal from the skies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In August 2026, an analysis of iron from ancient Greek tombs revealed surprising results. The objects surveyed included weapons and jewelry from around 3,000 to 4,000 years ago. Most of them were fashioned from regular old iron ore, but around 10 rings were made of iron from outer space—aka from meteorites that crash-landed on Earth.

It seems that, among the upper classes of Bronze Age Greece, rings fashioned from this out-of-this-world metal were all the rage. Before people learned how to extract iron from ore by melting it at super-high temperatures—a process called smelting—the only source of metallic iron was the occasional space rock. This material, known as meteoric iron, is rare worldwide, but especially in Greece, where approaching meteors usually disappear into the sea rather than make landfall.

Researchers believe that the Greek meteoric rings were actually imported from Egypt: a land with a special relationship to this metal from the skies.

Sources indicate that meteoric iron can be identified because it’s purer than the iron ore that naturally occurs on Earth, with a higher proportion of nickel mixed into it. Because meteoric iron “already arrives on Earth in metallic form,” indicates Victoria Almansa-Villatoro, a professor of Egyptology at Yale University, “it’s very malleable” and can be shaped more easily than unrefined ore.

According to recent reports, the Egyptians started working with this rare material early. “The oldest meteoric iron objects in the world come from Egypt,” indicates Almansa-Villatoro: Nine small beads, excavated from a site called Gerzeh along the bank of the Nile about 20 miles south of Cairo, are the oldest artifacts discovered made from space rocks. They are dated to around 3,200 BCE, more than a thousand years older than the 10 meteoric iron rings found in Greece.

According to recent reports, not only are the Gerzeh beads older than any other meteoric iron objects, they are much, much older than widespread iron smelting in Egypt. Almansa-Villatoro explains that “Egypt was relatively late in comparison with other Near Eastern civilizations to start smelting iron.” By the time the Egyptians were producing iron on a large scale in the 500s BCE, ancient people in Anatolia and other regions had been doing it for about five hundred years.

Industry observers note that A major reason for this late adoption was Egypt’s natural resources. Iron smelting forges burned a lot of wood charcoal, and Egypt had no large forests. For centuries, the Egyptians relied on bronze, which cost less fuel to produce. It wasn’t until major changes in political and trade networks, including pressure to match the iron arsenals of foreign enemies like the Assyrians, that the Egyptians finally made the shift.

Sources indicate that while early iron weapons and armor were not automatically better than bronze ones, iron proved easier to repair, and could be strengthened through further reworking. But objects like the Gerzeh beads show that the ancient Egyptians shaped small amounts of meteoric iron long before they knew how to extract it from ore.

In a recent development, the Gerzeh iron beads were incorporated into jewelry with gems and gold, hinting at their perceived value. All of the other Egyptian objects believed to be made of meteoric iron are similarly small and mostly decorative. The largest and most spectacular is a dagger with a meteoric iron blade more than eight inches long. It was found in the tomb of Egypt’s famous pharaoh, Tutankhamun, who died around 1,323 BCE.

Industry observers note that government records from the reign of Tutankhamun’s grandfather, Amenhotep III, mention an Anatolian king gifting a dagger to the Pharaoh. “People have speculated that this was the same dagger,” indicates Almansa-Villatoro. “Because, why would they make such a big deal about this king receiving a dagger from a foreign leader, unless it’s made of a very key or very rare material?” As seen with the recent findings from Greece, demand for meteoric iron in the ancient Mediterranean was international.

Recent findings suggest that as of 2013, archaeologists had discovered 28 objects in Egypt believed to be made of meteoric iron. This accounts for about half of the 55 known ancient meteoric iron artifacts found across Europe, Asia, and Africa as of 2023.

The prevalence of meteoric iron in Egypt is difficult to determine, as the composition of many iron objects has never been evaluated. Additionally, says Almansa-Villatoro, “we find more things in Egypt in general from this time period than in other regions,” due to the long history of archaeology there.

Recent findings suggest that analysis has shown that some of the Egyptian meteoric iron objects are made from several small meteorites combined. This might suggest that the Egyptians were “harvesting” and “actively looking” for this rare material, states Almansa-Villatoro, rather than just using it at random when a meteorite happened to land nearby.

Almansa-Villatoro believes that meteoric iron “was valuable because it was recognized to be material that came from the sky,” not just because it was more pure than other iron. Ancient Egyptian religious texts link iron with the heavens and the spiritual realm of the gods, who were sometimes described as having iron bones. One Egyptian term for iron literally translates to “the iron of the sky.“.

It has been revealed that “Some tools made of meteoric iron were used in a very crucial funerary ritual known as ‘the Opening of the Mouth,’” notes Almansa-Villatoro. These include small iron blades found in Tutankhamun’s tomb (though not the famous dagger). The purpose of this ritual was “to give the deceased back their senses,” Almansa-Villatoro explains, allowing them to speak, breathe, and eat in the afterlife. Meteoric iron might have been particularly prized for crafting these ritual objects.

By the time of Tutankhamun’s reign, the Egyptians might have encountered smelted iron produced in other lands, but they were still using meteoric iron in rituals and reverently placing it in tombs.

“It is possible that they still saw meteoric iron as something different” from smelted iron, notes Almansa-Villatoro, though it’s hard to say for sure.

Ancient Greece’s most famous oracle was just high on gas fumes.

In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution.

Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy.

At Scotland’s ancient Cladh Hallan, homes were full of human bones.

7 ways toilets have killed people.

For ancient Romans, pooping was a group activity.

Some Egyptian texts describe a dome of water with an iron shell enclosing the Earth. Meteoric iron might have been explained as fragments of this cosmic shell breaking off and falling to the Earth.

It’s clear that the Egyptians considered meteoric iron to be a special material, but what exactly they knew or didn’t know about it is not always easy to figure out. The Egyptians understood and interpreted the world around them using very different methods from our own. While we rely on experimental data documented in writing, ancient Egypt “was very much an oral society, where knowledge was transmitted through ritual and through recitation of texts,” says Almansa-Villatoro.

In ancient Egypt, “things that we wouldn’t consider science nowadays, like myth, could have fulfilled the same function” as science does today, states Almansa-Villatoro. The Egyptians used narrative myths to describe the physical universe. The iron shell surrounding the Earth appears in accounts of the soul’s journey to the afterlife, as a barrier that the spirits of the dead must sail across to reach the skies.

Recent findings suggest that with our modern knowledge, it’s easy to explain how a space rock might land on Earth. But what if all you knew of outer space was what you could see with your eyes from our planet’s surface? Egyptian myths may not have the structure of a modern scientific paper, but they offer a glimpse into how ancient people made sense of awe-inspiring natural phenomena like metal falling from the skies.

#224326. BYD in talks to buy Ineos’ French factory as Grenadier moves to US

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1228 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

BYD in talks to buy Ineos’ French factory as Grenadier moves to US

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.
  • BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France.
  • Industry observers note that the other half of the deal is Ineos packing up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The French factory Mercedes built for the tiny Smart city car, and that Jim Ratcliffe turned into the home of his Land Rover Defender tribute, could soon be building BYDs.

BYD confirmed today that it has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire Ineos Automotive’s plant in Hambach, France. If it closes, it would be the Chinese giant’s second passenger car factory in the EU after Hungary, and the first time a Chinese automaker buys an existing car plant in Europe.

Industry observers note that the other half of the deal is Ineos packing up. Alongside the announcement, Ineos Automotive mentioned it prepares to move Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the US, which it states accounts for about 70% of its sales. It has shortlisted US sites, hasn’t named any, and is aiming to start production there in 2028.

According to recent reports, the math is simple. Every Grenadier shipped from France to the US gets hit with a 15% tariff, and the Quartermaster pickup falls under the 25% tariff on imported pickups. When 7 out of 10 of your customers are American, building your trucks in Lorraine stops making sense.

Ineos indicates it will keep building both models at Hambach “for the medium term” if the sale goes through, so the two companies would share the site for a while.

Neither side disclosed a price or a closing date, and the sale still has to go through consultation with employee representatives. BYD will soon find out that France is nothing like China when it comes to employee representation. There’s also no word yet on which BYD models would come out of Hambach or when. Same for the plant’s roughly 1,000 employees: BYD made no commitment on how many it would keep.

BYD executive vice president Stella Li stated the company wants to give European consumers “vehicles built in France” that use BYD’s technology.

Recent findings suggest that hambach opened in 1997 as “Smartville,” Mercedes’ factory for the Smart Fortwo, and it later built the all-electric Smart EQ Fortwo. Ineos bought it from Mercedes at the end of 2020 after dropping its initiative to build a new factory in Wales, and Grenadier production started in 2022. Ineos says it has put nearly €540 million into the site since 2019.

Capacity is about 30,000 Grenadiers a year. That’s not much by BYD’s standards. BYD sold 3,561,615 passenger vehicles globally in the first 10 months of the year, which means 30,000 units is less than three days of its output.

There’s also a bit of irony in who’s buying. Ineos unveiled its first EV, the Fusilier, in early 2024 while romanticizing gas cars at the same event. A few months later, it shelved the electric model indefinitely, blaming “reluctant consumer uptake” of EVs. Now it’s selling its only factory to the world’s largest EV maker.

Industry observers note that this isn’t a surprise. Back in May, Stella Li remarked BYD was in talks with Stellantis and “other companies too” to take over underused plants in Europe, and that BYD would rather own and run a plant than form a joint venture. Hambach fits that description exactly.

BYD’s first European car plant, in Szeged, Hungary, started trial production earlier this year and is expected to reach mass production in early 2027, with the Dolphin Surf and Atto 2 first in line. BYD eventually wants more than 150,000 vehicles a year out of it. Its separate factory project in Turkey has been put on pause.

The motivation is regulatory. China-built BYD EVs face a 17% countervailing duty in the EU on top of the standard 10% car tariff, imported Chinese hybrids are now subject to quotas, and the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules would tie EV subsidies and public contracts to how much of a vehicle is built locally. A French plant solves a lot of those problems at once.

Industry observers note that and BYD isn’t alone. Leapmotor started building the B10 at Stellantis’ Zaragoza plant in Spain in October, Dongfeng plans to build cars at a Stellantis factory in France, Geely is reportedly lining up a Ford plant in Spain, and Chery already assembles vehicles in Barcelona.

Chery is the one BYD should watch. Through October, BYD registered 320,445 vehicles in Europe, up 133%, according to Automotive News. Chery Group was just ahead with 320,631, up 235%. A gap of 186 cars.

Recent findings suggest that europe matters more than ever for BYD because home isn’t going well. BYD brand sales in China fell 40% to 1,544,699 vehicles over the first 10 months, and its global passenger vehicle sales are down 2.7%.

Industry observers note that this is a smart, cheap move for BYD. Building Szeged took years, including land disputes with private owners. Hambach comes with a trained workforce, a paint shop, a supplier base on the German border, and a seller that’s motivated to leave. You don’t get a much easier entry into France, but the easiest in France is still probably more difficult than anything BYD faced in China when it comes to deploying fresh production capacity.

The 30,000-unit capacity is small, but BYD isn’t buying it for what it builds today. It’s buying a “Made in France” label ahead of local content rules.

Recent findings suggest that I'm guessing BYD is gambling on the French not making it too difficult as it would deter future investment. They're probably also going to use a lot of robots.

We also can’t ignore the symmetry here. Ineos is leaving Europe to build in the US because of tariffs. BYD is buying into Europe because of tariffs. That’s protectionism moving factories. Europe keeps the jobs, and the workers who used to build Smart EVs might get to build EVs again.

And yes, it’s funny that BYD is moving into the home of the Grenadier, a vehicle that exists because Ratcliffe loved the old Defender, days after a court in The Hague barred BYD’s Ti7 from the EU for infringing Land Rover’s Defender design.

The real question is what BYD puts on the line in Hambach. If it’s battery-electric cars, great. If it’s plug-in hybrids built to get around quotas, Europe is trading one gas-burning 4×4 factory for another.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first latest arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

It has been revealed that speaking of elemental reactions, newly introduced in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

In a recent development, then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

It has been revealed that luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

Recent findings suggest that the first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a newly introduced outfit in the shop at a discount.

Industry observers note that version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

Recent findings suggest that all around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

Finally, you can look forward to the upcoming Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.
